A1|tenses|Present tense: one form for every person|19,20,15,822,833,840,841,1233,2008|Danish verbs have just one present form for all persons: add -er or -r to the stem.|Good news: in the present tense a Danish verb does **not** change with the subject.¶T:Infinitive¦Present//at tale (to speak)¦jeg, du, han, vi, de **taler**//at bo (to live)¦jeg, du, han, vi, de **bor**//at lære (to learn)¦jeg, du, han, vi, de **lærer**¶The infinitive ends in **-e** (at tale). To get the present, add **-r** to verbs ending in -e (tale → taler), and **-er** to the stem of other verbs (spis → spiser). Some short verbs add nothing or -r: bo → bor, gå → går.¶• Jeg **taler** lidt dansk. (I speak a little Danish.)¶• Hun **bor** i Denver. (She lives in Denver.)¶• **Spiller** du tennis? (Do you play tennis?)¶**Tip:** there are no -s endings like English "he speaks". Irregular verbs like være (er) and have (har) also use one form for all persons.
A1|tenses|Present tense means "I do" and "I am doing"|820,827,834,1237,1629,825,841,840|The Danish present covers both English "I cook" and "I am cooking".|English has two present tenses (I cook / I am cooking). Danish has only one:¶• Jeg **laver** mad i dag. (I am cooking today.)¶• Jeg **læser** en bog. (I am reading a book.)¶• Jeg **hører** musik. (I am listening to music.)¶• Jeg **sover** allerede. (I am already sleeping.)¶The same form also expresses habits: Jeg **laver** mad hver dag. (I cook every day.)¶**Common mistake:** do not try to build "am cooking" with være + verb. Danish has no -ing form; the present tense does the whole job. The English "-ing" form is usually translated with the infinitive or by a plain present: Jeg kan godt lide at lave mad. (I like cooking.)¶If you want to stress that something is going on right now, add lige nu (right now): Jeg laver lige nu mad.
A1|tenses|Present tense for the future|1630,2425,2015,2435,4031,2420,1640,35|Danish often uses the present tense for the future, especially with a time word.|To talk about the future, Danish usually uses the **present tense** plus a time word:¶• Jeg **ringer** til dig senere. (I will call you later.)¶• Toget **kører** klokken ti. (The train leaves at ten.)¶• Vi **ses** i morgen! (See you tomorrow!)¶• Jeg **flyver** til Wien. (I am flying to Vienna.)¶This is perfectly normal for plans, schedules and promises. You can also use skal for definite plans (Jeg skal rejse i morgen) or vil for intentions and predictions (Det vil regne i morgen). In everyday speech, the present is enough.¶**Tip for English speakers:** English "will" is not translated word for word. Do not say "Jeg vil ringe" if you only mean a plain future: that means "I want to call".
A1|tenses|Perfect tense: har + participle|2412,876,879,1655,2479,54,1656,3280,2864|The perfect is har + past participle (-et or -t): jeg har spist, jeg har boet.|The perfect tense talks about the past with a link to now, and it is the usual way to say "I have ..." or "I did ...":¶**har + past participle**¶T:Infinitive¦participle¦example//at hente¦hentet¦Jeg har hentet rundstykker.//at sove¦sovet¦Jeg har sovet dårligt.//at reservere¦reserveret¦Jeg har reserveret et værelse.//at få¦fået¦Jeg har fået jobbet!//at tage¦taget¦Jeg har taget på.¶Regular verbs: **-e → -et** (for most verbs: lave → lavet) or **-t** (for some: bo → boet, spise → spist). Irregular verbs have special participles: have → haft, være → været, få → fået.¶• Jeg **har været** i Paris før. (I have been to Paris before.)¶• Jeg **har bestilt** den online. (I ordered it online.)¶The participle goes to the end of the clause, and har stays in second position.
A1|tenses|Perfect with er: er faret, er blevet, er kommet|2426,483,883,3244,3263,1660,5192,5528|With verbs of motion and change, Danish uses er instead of har: er blevet, er kommet.|Most verbs form the perfect with **har**, but verbs that express **movement or a change of state** use **er**:¶• Jeg **er** faret vild. (I have driven the car.) Jeg er kørt til byen. (I drove to town.) Some verbs, such as løbe or flyve, use either depending on whether a destination is mentioned.¶**Tip:** if you are unsure, har is usually right, but with komme, blive and rejse, remember er.

A1|tenses|Past tense of være and have: var and havde|2480,2486,2490,1259,514,3734,65,3686|The past of være is var and the past of have is havde: one form for every person.|The simple past, also called the preterite, is used for finished actions, and it also has one form for all persons.¶T:Infinitive¦present¦past//være (be)¦er¦var//have (have)¦har¦havde¦• Vejret **var** super. A1|order|Verb second (V2) in statements|15,19,403,435,807,822,1602,1606,2419,2425|In Danish main clauses the verb is always the second element.|The most important word order rule: the **finite verb comes second** in a statement. The first position can be the subject, but also something else.¶T:1st¦2nd (verb)¦rest//Jeg¦bor¦i Denver.//Vi¦har¦en hund.//Toget¦kører¦klokken ti.¶• Jeg **bor** i Denver. (I live in Denver.)¶• Jeg **står** op klokken syv. (I get up at seven.)¶• Jeg **arbejder** som lærer. (I work as a teacher.)¶• Vi **har** en hund. (We have a dog.)¶If a clause has two verbs (modal or perfect), the first one is in second position, and the other goes to the end: Jeg **har** hentet rundstykker. Jeg **kan** ikke sove.¶**Tip:** English allows "Tomorrow I go ..." with the same order as Danish, but Danish is stricter and always needs the verb in position two.
A1|order|Inversion: verb before subject after a time word|4007,4039,4040,4009,1631,2421,2838,4006|If something other than the subject comes first, the verb still stays second: I dag har jeg ikke tid.|When you start the sentence with a time word, a place or an object, the verb stays in second place and the subject moves **after** the verb (inversion):¶T:1st¦verb¦subject//Jeg¦har¦ikke tid i dag.//I dag¦har¦jeg ikke tid.//Om sommeren¦rejser¦jeg væk.¶• **I dag har jeg** ikke tid. (I do not have time today.)¶• **Om sommeren rejser jeg** væk. (In the summer I go away.)¶• **Om vinteren er det** koldt. (It is cold in winter.)¶• **Her er** mit pas. (Here is my passport.)¶**Common mistake:** keeping the English order: "I dag jeg har ikke tid" is wrong. The verb has to be second, so the subject comes after.

A1|order|Where ikke and other adverbs go|1681,464,2847,1215,2036,3810,98,2111,1216|In a main clause ikke, aldrig, altid and bare come right after the verb.|In a simple main clause, **ikke** and short adverbs come **after the verb**:¶• Jeg spiser **ikke** kød. A1|order|Subordinate clauses: ikke before the verb|5644,5243,5514,5871,6236,6392,6015|In clauses starting with at, hvis, som etc., ikke comes before the verb: at du ikke har.|In a **main clause** ikke comes after the verb: Du **har ikke** sproget. A1|verbs|Present of være and have: er and har|17,16,824,1203,1609,403,404,405,1605,3202|Er and har are the present of være (be) and have (have).|The two most important Danish verbs are irregular. A1|modal|Polite requests with kan, kunne and vil gerne|85,49,50,55,201,1253,1241,1231,213|Kunne du ...? and Må jeg ...? are polite; add lige and tak to soften them.|To make polite requests, Danish uses these patterns:¶• **Kan** du ...? A1|articles|Two genders: en and et|435,841,803,1232,802,1201,1206,1207,1209,1624|Every Danish noun is either en (common gender) or et (neuter); you have to learn the article with the word.|Danish has just **two genders**: common gender (**en**) and neuter (**et**). A1|articles|The definite form: -en and -et|812,814,837,1236,835,845,821,1607,2401,801|Danish adds the definite article to the end of the noun: bogen, huset (the book, the house).|In English "the" comes before the noun. A1|conj|Og and eller: and, or|861,1272,1248,2422,1276,1195,8,64|Og = and, eller = or; they join words, phrases and sentences without changing word order.|**Og** (and) and **eller** (or) join words, groups and clauses. A2|tenses|Talking about plans: skal + infinitive|2812,2070,2481,4045,1654,3259,3271,450,2419,4012|Skal + a place or an infinitive expresses plans and obligations; the present tense is also used for arranged events.|To talk about **plans and arrangements**, Danish uses **skal** or just the present tense.¶• **Skal + verb**: Vi **skal** ud at vandre i weekenden. A2|tenses|Future with the present tense, vil and kommer til at|35,476,885,2078,2883,4006,6029,6031|Danish has no future tense: use the present with a time word, vil for prediction, kommer til at for what will happen.|There is no separate future tense in Danish. A2|modal|Polite past forms: ville, kunne, skulle|94,107,209,512,548,925,228,1256,49,3664|Ville, kunne and skulle in the past form are used to be polite or to express wishes and hypotheticals.|The past forms of the modals (**ville, kunne, skulle**) are also used to sound **polite or tentative**, even when you mean the present.¶T:Plain¦Softer//Jeg vil gerne … (I want)¦Jeg ville gerne … (I'd like)//Kan du …?¦Kunne du …?//Jeg skal …¦Jeg skulle …¶• Jeg **ville** bare sige, at jeg er glad. A2|articles|Two genders: en and et|1207,2429,2808,39,2436,803,4036,1206|Danish nouns are either common gender (en) or neuter (et); you have to learn the gender with each noun.|Danish has only **two genders**: common gender (**en**) and neuter (**et**). Gender decides the definite ending, the possessives (min/mit) and adjective agreement (stor/stort), so a wrong gender spreads through the whole phrase.
A2|articles|Definite form: the article goes on the end|1236,837,812,814,821,1229,445,2842,474|The Danish for 'the' is a suffix: -en on en-words, -et on et-words, -ne/-erne in the plural.|In English 'the' stands in front. A2|articles|No article: jobs, nationalities and mass nouns|1603,1609,1602,433,1233,2831|Leave out en/et with professions, nationalities and unspecified amounts of things like water, tea or rice.|Danish drops the indefinite article in places where English keeps 'a'.¶• **Jobs and roles** after at være or at arbejde som: **Jeg er ingeniør.** (I'm an engineer.) **Min tante er læge.** (My aunt is a doctor.)¶• **Nationalities and religions** used as a noun: Han er dansker. A2|articles|En and én: 'one' vs 'a', and containers|1206,1238,1239,1240,1222,2814,874,5988,6385|En/et means 'a'; stressed én/ét means 'one'. The accent on én/ét is optional unless the sentence would be unclear.
A2|nouns|Indefinite plurals: -er, -e and -r|4035,3219,3249,2074,4081,2415,403,442,2013,828,4080,2882|Most Danish nouns form the plural by adding -er (after consonant), -r (after -e) or -e (some words).|Danish has three common plural endings. A2|nouns|Neuter nouns: plural -er or no ending|410,412,828,4062,456,1668,5547,5677|Many neuter nouns, especially one-syllable ones, keep the same form in the plural: et år – to år.|Neuter (et) nouns often behave differently from en-words in the plural.¶• Many one-syllable neuter nouns have **no plural ending**: **et år – to år, et dyr – to dyr, et ord – to ord, et bord – to bord, et glas – to glas**.¶• Neuter nouns ending in -e or a longer stem take **-r** or **-er**: et værelse – værelser, et æble – æbler.¶• **Børn** (children) is irregular: et barn – børn.¶• Min datter er fem **år** gammel. (I have worked here for three years.)¶**Tip:** after a number the noun is plural, but a word like år does not change: say **to år**, never to års or to åre. Do not add English-style -s.
A2|nouns|Definite plural: -ne, -ene and -erne|445,2842,474,865,855,2483,459,1649,4086,3256,3257,2883,5540,5292|In the plural the article ending is -ne (after -e), -ene (after -er-less words) or -erne (after -er plurals).|To make the definite plural, look at how the indefinite plural ends:¶T:Plural ends in¦definite plural¦example//-er¦add -ne¦venner – venner**ne**, planter – planter**ne**//-e¦add -ne¦heste – heste**ne**, dage – dage**ne**//no ending¦add -ene¦børn – børn**ene**, sko – sko**ene**, år – år**ene**¶• Hvor er **børnene**? A2|nouns|Irregular plurals: mand – mænd, bog – bøger|409,2415,410,403,823,470,485,5861,579,5863,5741,6396,5859,5867|A small group of everyday nouns changes their vowel or ending in the plural and must be learned by heart.|A number of common nouns are irregular – and they are mostly the ones you need first.¶T:Singular¦plural//en mand¦mænd//en bog¦bøger//en fod¦fødder//en hånd¦hænder//en tand¦tænder//et barn¦børn//et øje¦øjne//en bror¦brødre//en nat¦nætter//en by¦byer¶• Jeg har to **brødre**. A2|pronouns|Personal pronouns: jeg/mig, du/dig, han/ham|8,811,419,420,11,1209,85,441,3640,424,1630,2849,4066,2870,472|Danish personal pronouns have a subject form (jeg, du, han) and an object form (mig, dig, ham).|Danish personal pronouns change form depending on whether they are the **subject** or the **object** (after a verb or preposition).¶T:Subject¦Object//jeg¦mig//du¦dig//han¦ham//hun¦hende//den/det¦den/det//vi¦os//I¦jer//de¦dem¶• **Jeg** elsker **dig**. A2|pronouns|Possessives: min bog, mit hus, mine børn|1631,2421,443,433,1244,401,402,418,427,2439,414,415|Danish possessives agree with the thing owned: min (en-word), mit (et-word), mine (plural).|Danish possessives agree with the **noun they describe**, not with the owner.¶T:en-word¦et-word¦plural//min¦mit¦mine (my)//din¦dit¦dine (your)//vores¦vores¦vores (our)//jeres¦jeres¦jeres (your, plural)¶**Hans** (his), **hendes** (her), **deres** (their) never change.¶• Det her er **min** mor. A2|pronouns|Reflexive possessives: sin, sit, sine|466,5738,5177,5450,5680,6008,5682,6289,5284,798,5481,5353|Use sin/sit/sine when the owner is the subject of the sentence, and hans/hendes when it is someone else.|When 'his/her/its/their' refers back to the **subject of the same clause**, Danish uses the reflexive possessive **sin / sit / sine** (agreeing with the thing owned, like min/mit/mine).¶T:Meaning¦Danish//his own father (subject = he)¦Han ligner **sin** far.//another person's father¦Han ligner **hans** far. (You have to cite your sources.)¶**Rules:** sin/sit/sine are used only for the third person (han, hun, den/det, de, man) and always refer back to the subject. A2|pronouns|This, that and which: denne, dette, hvilken|2424,401,414,1221,2441,2437,4008,4010,1285,2824,6029,6326|Den/det her points to something near, hvilken/hvilket asks 'which'; both agree with the noun's gender.|**Demonstratives** point to things; they agree with the noun's gender and number.¶T:Meaning¦en-word¦et-word¦plural//this¦den her / denne¦det her / dette¦de her / disse//that¦den der¦det der¦de der¶In everyday speech **den her / det her / de her** (this/these) and **den der / det der / de der** (that/those) are the normal forms; **denne / dette / disse** are more formal.¶• Er **den her** plads ledig? A2|pronouns|Reflexive pronouns: mig, dig, sig|3623,3250,3659,3645,484,5359,811,4058,5990,5645,1249|After a reflexive verb the object points back to the subject: mig, dig, sig, os, jer, sig.|A **reflexive pronoun** refers back to the subject. A2|adjectives|Adjective agreement before a noun: stor, stort, store|802,423,2835,1624,2031,2885,1673,2088,478,1686,2863,483|After en/et the adjective adds nothing for en-words, -t for et-words and -e in the plural.|An adjective placed before an indefinite noun agrees with it in gender and number.¶T:en-word¦et-word¦plural//en stor bil¦et stort hus¦store biler//en ny ven¦et nyt job¦nye venner//en god dag¦et godt køb¦gode dage¶• Vi er **en stor** familie. A2|adjectives|Adjectives after verbs: Det er koldt, Skoene er flotte|814,1229,2803,2842,818,866,3605,2024,3607,2066,3608,3616|After er/var the adjective agrees with the subject: stor, stort or store; Det er … always takes -t.|After verbs like **være** (to be) and **blive** (to become) the adjective agrees with the **subject**, just as it does before a noun.¶• en-word subject: **Stuen er stor.** (The living room is big.) **Maden er kold.** (The food is cold.)¶• et-word subject: Huset er **stort**. A2|adjectives|Adjectives that do not take -t|3617,1621,3655,2467,6378,5596,2909,3020,5756,5491|Adjectives ending in -sk, -ende, -et or -s stay unchanged in the neuter form.|Many adjectives can't take an extra **-t** in the neuter form.¶• **-ende**: Arbejdet er spændende. A2|preps|Direction and origin: til, fra, hos|13,2440,2419,2482,3269,463,481,461,3243,431,1662,2082|Til means 'to', fra means 'from', hos means 'at someone's place' or 'with' a person.|Three small words describe movement and origin:¶• **Til** = to (where you are going): Jeg tager **til** Berlin. A2|preps|Other common prepositions: med, uden, for, af, mod, om|1224,1223,441,1253,489,440,2802,2826,3620,3644,3222,2831,3640,2029|A handful of small prepositions appear in fixed phrases; learn them together with the verb or adjective.|Many Danish verbs and adjectives require a particular preposition, which often differs from English.¶T:Preposition¦Meaning¦Example//**med**¦with, by (means)¦Med mælk, tak. Kan jeg betale **med** kort?//**uden**¦without¦**Uden** sukker.//**for**¦for, too¦Den er **for** dyr. (too expensive) Det er vigtigt **for** mig.//**af**¦of, by, from¦Jeg drikker masser **af** te. (Do you want to eat with us?)¶• Jeg er glad **for** det. (I'm glad about it.)¶• Jeg har brug **for** vand. (I need water.)¶• Tillykke **med** fødselsdagen! (Happy birthday!)¶**Tip:** learn the prepositions with the verb: glad **for**, ked **af**, tillykke **med**, brug **for**. English often uses a different word.
A2|conj|Og, men, eller: joining clauses|2422,1248,5344,5559,5965,5987,6284,861,5762,1276|Og, men and eller join words or main clauses; after them the verb stays in second position.|The coordinating conjunctions **og** (and), **men** (but), **eller** (or) and **for** (because) join words or whole main clauses.¶• Words: Vi mangler mælk **og** æg. (We need milk and eggs.) Enkelt **eller** retur? (One-way or round-trip?)¶• Clauses with **men**: Jeg forstår næsten alt, **men** det er svært for mig at tale. (I understand almost everything, but speaking is hard for me.) Historien gentager sig ikke, **men** den rimer. (History doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes.)¶• Clauses with **og**: Man bliver aldrig færdig med at lære, **og** det er det gode ved det. (You never stop learning, and that's the beauty of it.)¶**Word order:** after og/men/eller the clause keeps normal main-clause order (subject – verb). Jeg er træt, **men** jeg **kommer** alligevel.¶**Comma:** use a comma before men and before og/eller when it begins a new main clause with its own subject; no comma when the subject is shared: Jeg kommer og hjælper.¶**Tip:** og also joins two verbs of activity: Jeg tager ud og svømmer. (I go swimming.)
A2|conj|At: that-clauses|3270,3681,3813,5516,5511,6042,6044,6051,6059|At introduces a subordinate clause after verbs of saying, thinking and feeling. It cannot be left out.|**At** (that) introduces a **subordinate clause** after verbs like sige (say), tro (believe), vide (know), håbe (hope), and adjectives like glad (happy). In English 'that' is often omitted; in Danish at is always kept.¶• Lægen siger**, at** jeg skal hvile mig. (The doctor says I should rest.)¶• Jeg er glad for**, at** du er her. (I'm glad you're here.)¶• Jeg ved**, at** jeg intet ved. (I know that I know nothing.)¶• Jeg tvivler på**, at** det virker. (I doubt that will work.)¶• Det skyldes**, at** ingen har tid. (That's because nobody has time.)¶**Comma:** always put a comma before at.¶**Word order in the at-clause:** subject – adverb – verb: …, at du **ikke** kommer. Compare the main clause: Du kommer **ikke**.¶**Tip:** do not confuse **at** (that) with **at** (to, infinitive marker). Both are written the same way, but the conjunction is followed by a subject: Jeg håber, at jeg vinder. Jeg håber at vinde.
A2|conj|Hvis, når, mens, da: if and when|113,208,1006,4103,2221,2896,6342,6333|Hvis means 'if', når 'when' (present/future/habit), da 'when' (past, once), mens 'while'.|These subordinate conjunctions all need a comma and the word order subject – adverb – verb.¶T:Word¦Meaning¦Example//**hvis**¦if¦Hvis du har spørgsmål, er du velkommen til at kontakte os. (If you have questions, feel free to contact us.)//**når**¦when, whenever¦Sig til, **når** du har tid. (Get in touch when you have time.)//**da**¦when (once, in the past)¦Jeg brækkede armen, **da** jeg stod på ski. (I broke my arm skiing.)//**mens**¦while¦Kan du vande blomsterne, **mens** jeg er væk?¶**Når vs da:** når = repeated or future events (Når det regner, bliver jeg hjemme), da = a single event in the past.¶• Hvad laver du, **når** du ikke arbejder? (What do you do when you're not working?)¶• Den var allerede i stykker, **da** jeg købte den. (It was already broken when I bought it.)¶• **Mens** du laver mad, dækker jeg bord. (While you cook, I'll set the table.)¶**Inversion after a leading clause:** if the subordinate clause comes first, the main clause starts with the verb: **Hvis** du har tid, **kommer** jeg.
A2|conj|Der and som: relative clauses|6383,5244,5468,5306,6015,5648,6137,6211,5506,6036,6403,6283|Der or som replaces the subject of a relative clause; som alone can also be the object. (Publish or perish.)¶• Sidst, men ikke mindst, vil jeg takke alle, **der** har været med. (Last but not least, I thank everyone involved.)¶• Vi ses, **som** man så fint siger. (See you around, as they say.)¶**Rule:** use **der** when the relative word is the **subject** (of the clause); use **som** for the object. **Som** is also the 'as' of comparison and 'like'. A2|conj|Linking words: derfor, desuden, alligevel, dermed|6058,6052,6125,5934,6141,6150,5642,6037|Linking adverbs such as derfor and dermed connect sentences and take inversion: Derfor foreslår jeg …|Linking adverbs show how sentences relate (cause, addition, contrast). A2|neg|Ikke: negating a verb|880,1199,3237,42,1681,464,116,1400,2809|Ikke is placed after the finite verb in a main clause: Jeg kan ikke sove.|To negate a sentence, put **ikke** (not) in the sentence. Its position depends on the clause type:¶• **Main clause**: ikke comes **after the finite verb** (and after pronoun objects): Mit vækkeur ringede **ikke**. (My alarm didn't go off.) (I can't sleep.)¶• **In the perfect**: ikke comes before the participle: Jeg har **ikke** hørt vækkeuret. (I didn't hear the alarm.)¶• **Subordinate clauses**: ikke comes before the verb: …, at du **ikke** kommer.¶T:Positive¦Negative//Jeg kan sove.¦Jeg kan **ikke** sove.//Han er her.¦Han er **ikke** her.//Vi ses tit.¦Vi ses **ikke** så tit.¶**Tip:** there is no 'do not' – Danish says Jeg ved ikke, never Jeg gør ikke vide. For 'not any / no' use ingen/intet, see the next rule. Jeg forstyrrer vel ikke? uses vel to soften.

A2|punct|Compound nouns and hyphens|2820,801,2032,836,2413,2414,2010,2409,826,1627,2011,2811,434,2843,5912,5884,838|Danish writes compounds as one word (badeværelse). Add endings to English-style words with an apostrophe: wifi'en, cd'en.¶**Common mistake:** writing the parts separately is wrong, and the order is reversed from English: kaffekop (coffee cup) but en kop kaffe (a cup of coffee). A2|punct|Commas, question marks and quotation marks|1,3,29,41,47,50,64,3681,3270,2066,2476,5516,4069,1652|Danish has a comma before subordinate clauses (at, når, hvis …); questions end in ?, quotes use " " or » «.|A few basic punctuation rules for Danish:¶• **Question mark** at the end of a question: Hvad siger du? Kære modtager,¶• **Comma before a subordinate clause** (clause with at, fordi, når, hvis, mens, som, der): Lægen siger**,** at jeg skal hvile mig. Jeg er glad for**,** at du er her. Jeg tager ud og svømmer**,** når det er varmt.¶• A comma also separates two main clauses, such as in Ikke så meget**,** hvad med dig?¶• **Quotation marks**: Hvordan siger man "thank you" på dansk? B1|tenses|Past perfect: havde + participle|4105,3715,3961,5690,5921,5953,249,360|Havde (or var) plus the past participle shows that something happened before another moment in the past.|Use the **past perfect** for an event that lies before another event in the past. (We could not come.)¶Kunne with a request sounds softer than **kan**. Modal verbs are followed by a bare infinitive with no **at**. Common mistake: “Kan du at hjælpe mig?” Say “Kan du hjælpe mig?”. Tip: “Kunne jeg få ...?” is the standard way of ordering in cafés and shops.
B1|modal|Skal: must, shall and be supposed to|3298,110,121,846,850,875,887,897,901|Skal says that something is a duty or an arrangement, and shall we in questions.|**Skal** (present and infinitive form of "skulle") is a strong modal verb with several meanings.¶T:Meaning¦Example//duty, order¦Du skal sove.//plan, arrangement¦Jeg skal til tandlægen i morgen.//shall we...?¦Skal vi gå?//reported claim¦Han skal være rig.¶• **Skal** jeg hjælpe dig? (Shall I help you?)¶• Du **skal** ikke gå. (You should not go.)¶• Hvad **skal** du lave i weekenden? (What are you doing at the weekend?)¶Compare **skal ikke** (be told not to, or no intention) with **må ikke** (not allowed). Common mistake: using vil for plans, as in English "will". Danish uses skal for plans and arrangements. Tip: **skal** + a direction word often means "is going to": “Jeg skal til Odense”.
B1|modal|Må: may and must|159,169,243,55,115,201,1715,2844,2860|Må means may (permission) and must (necessity), depending on the context.|**Må** (infinitive: måtte) covers two ideas.¶T:Meaning¦Example//be allowed to¦Må jeg gå ud? (May I go out?)//have to¦Jeg må gå nu. (I have to go now.)//not allowed¦Du må ikke ryge her. (You must not smoke here.)¶• **Må** jeg spørge dig om noget? (May I ask you something?)¶• Jeg **må** hellere gå. (I had better go.)¶• Man **må** jo videre. (One has to go on.)¶Context decides. A question starting with **må jeg** is normally a polite request. A statement with må is often a necessity. Common mistake: using må to mean "might". For possibility use **kan** or **måske**. Tip: **må** is a short, friendly form, whereas **skal** feels stronger.
B1|modal|Necessity: nødt til at, behøver ikke at, må ikke|111,1706,2094,4054,3891,5607,5777,3651,2809|Er nødt til at means have to; behøver ikke at means not necessary; må ikke forbids.|Danish has several ways to say "have to", and the negatives are easy to mix up.¶T:Phrase¦Meaning¦Example//er nødt til at¦have to, be forced to¦Jeg er nødt til at gå.//behøver ikke at¦does not need to¦Du behøver ikke at komme.//skal ikke¦should not / no need¦Du skal ikke bekymre dig.//må ikke¦is not allowed to¦Du må ikke parkere her.¶• Jeg **er** desværre **nødt til at** gå nu. Tip: **er nødt til at** is very common in speech, with the future form **bliver nødt til at** (will have to).
B1|modal|Burde and bør: should|518,1317,2113,3314,3417,1739,1860,1003,5177|Burde and bør give advice and say what would be sensible or right.|**Bør** (present) and **burde** (past form, used as a softer present) give advice.¶• Du **bør** tale med din læge. (One should spread one's money.)¶**Burde** is the more usual form in conversation and sounds gentler than **bør**. Tip: with a negative, “Du **bør** ikke ...” is mild, and “Du **må** ikke ...” is a ban.
B1|modal|Vil gerne: polite wishes|1252,1334,1347,2449,2893,3037,925,512,626|Vil gerne (would like) is the standard polite way to order, ask or state a wish.|**Vil gerne** (literally "want gladly") is the standard way to say "I would like".¶• Jeg **vil gerne** have en kaffe. Tip: **have** after vil gerne means "get/take", and a verb gives the action.

B1|modal|Vil and ville: wanting|441,221,94,209,548,1001,1205,1321,2628|Vil expresses wishes and intentions; ville is its past form.|**Vil** means "want to" in the present, and **ville** is the past form.¶• **Vil** du spise med os? B1|nouns|Genitive -s: showing possession|697,3330,1402,2247,5623,2163,1006,1251,1333|Add -s to a noun, with no apostrophe, to show who owns it: Annes bil.|Danish has no real cases, but it does have a genitive -s that shows possession. B1|nouns|Compound nouns: one word, last part decides|1087,2470,1889,438,439,449,1002,1026,1200|Danish glues nouns into one word, sometimes with a linking -s or -e, and the last part gives the gender.|Danish writes compounds as **one word**, where English often uses two. Tip: when you meet a long word, cut it from the right: the last part tells you what it is, the first part tells you what kind.

B1|pronouns|Reflexive possessive: sin, sit, sine|466,496,503,642,798,6008,794,5177,5214|Use sin/sit/sine when the owner is the subject; use hans/hendes/deres for someone else.|When the owner is a **singular third-person subject** (han, hun, man, den, det) of the same clause, Danish uses a reflexive possessive: **sin** (en-words), **sit** (et-words), **sine** (plural nouns). (One should spread one's money.)¶Compare: "Peter besøger **sin** bror" (his own brother) and "Peter besøger **hans** bror" (someone else's brother). With a plural subject Danish uses deres: "De elsker deres børn". Sin/sit/sine is never part of the subject itself: "Han og hans bror" is correct. Common mistake: using sin for someone else, which makes the sentence unclear.

B1|particles|Bare: only and just|94,114,130,209,242,920,937,1012,1425|Bare limits things (only) and softens commands and complaints (just).|**Bare** is one of the most flexible Danish words.¶T:Use¦Example//just, merely¦Det var bare for sjov.//softening a command¦Skriv bare en besked til mig.//just wanted to¦Jeg ville bare sige tak.//never, only¦Jeg får bare aldrig pudset vinduer.¶• Jeg ville **bare** sige, at jeg er glad. B1|particles|Lige, egentlig and altså|204,279,115,201,209,353,2354,50|Lige (just, quickly), egentlig (actually) and altså (so, I mean) soften questions and add nuance.|These three fillers appear in everyday speech.¶T:Word¦Effect¦Example//lige¦just, quickly, for a moment¦Må jeg lige forstyrre dig?//egentlig¦actually, really¦Hvordan kender du egentlig Lisa?//altså¦I mean, so, really (emphasis)¦Nu går det altså for vidt!¶• Må jeg **lige** præsentere mig? B2|tenses|Present perfect or simple past (har gjort / gjorde)|878,1344,1724,1823,2221,2488,2896,3016|Perfect = result or link to now; simple past = a finished event placed at a specific time. (Can you leave out the onions?)¶• **Lad os** + infinitive is the usual let us; it is also a gentle imperative.¶• The same bare infinitive follows other perception verbs: Jeg hører ham synge. Jeg ser dig komme.¶• Mistake: Lad os at gå.

(I assembled the shelf myself.)¶Examples with selve: Sprog lærer man bedst i **selve** landet. (You learn languages best in the country itself.) Litteraturlisten var længere end **selve** opgaven. (The bibliography was longer than the thesis itself.) Det rammer **selve** kernen i problemet. (That hits the very core of the problem.)¶• Selv stands next to the word it stresses, often right after the subject or at the end: Jeg skal **selv** betale en del.¶• Selve is always followed by a definite noun, so selve kernen, not selve kerne.¶• Selv can also mean even: **Selv** den længste rejse begynder med et skridt. This is different from selvom (even though).¶• Tip: reflexive plus selv, as in til mig selv, is covered in the reflexives rule.
B2|pronouns|Reciprocal pronoun hinanden|98,136,202,235,454,455,491,529,535,566|Hinanden means each other and is the object of reciprocal verbs and prepositions.|**Hinanden** is the Danish for each other and one another. It works as a direct object or after a preposition, and always refers to two or more people.¶Examples: Vi har ikke set **hinanden** i lang tid. (We have not seen each other for a long time.) Hvordan mødte I **hinanden**? (How did you two meet?) Så har vi vist misforstået **hinanden**. (Then we seem to have misunderstood each other.) Vi har kendt **hinanden** siden skoletiden. (We have known each other since school.) Vi gik fra **hinanden** som gode venner. (We broke up as good friends.)¶• With a preposition it is written as two words: **til hinanden**, **med hinanden**, **fra hinanden**.¶• Genitive: hinandens, as in Vi hjælper **hinandens** børn.¶• Do not use sig here: De mødte sig is wrong; say De mødte hinanden.¶• Some verbs are already reciprocal in meaning with a plural subject: De mødes. (They meet.)¶• Tip: if you can replace it with each other in English, use hinanden.
B2|pronouns|Generic man: you do what you can|281,283,684,1120,1167,1385,1505,1522,1595,2717|Man means one/you in general; use it for rules and common experience, not for a specific person.|**Man** is the general subject: one, you, people. It is used for rules, common experience, advice and sayings. It is written with a small m except at the start of a sentence, and it takes the same verb forms as other 3rd-person subjects.¶Examples: **Man** gør, hvad man kan. (You do what you can.) **Man** må jo videre. (You have to move on.) **Man** er, hvad man spiser. (You are what you eat.) **Man** skal have visum for at rejse ind. (You need a visa to enter.) Det er i nøden, **man** kender sine venner. (A friend in need is a friend indeed.)¶• Man cannot be an object. Use en (accusative) or dig: Det gør **en** glad. (It makes you happy.)¶• Man replaces the passive in everyday Danish: **Man** taler dansk her. (Danish is spoken here.)¶• If you mean a specific person, use du, ham, hende. Man is vague.¶• English speakers often overuse you; Danish prefers man for rules, and du for direct advice to a listener.
B2|pronouns|Indefinites: nogen, noget, ingen, ingenting|63,128,269,832,2714,2839,3796,4154,4283,1386|Nogen = someone/any, noget = something/any, ingen = no one/none, ingenting or intet = nothing; also used in questions.|These pronouns are very frequent. **Nogen** (people, or common nouns), **noget** (things, or neuter nouns), **ingen** (nobody, no + common or plural noun), **intet** or **ingenting** (nothing).¶Examples: Er der **nogen**? (Is anyone there?) **Nogen** har stjålet min pung. (Somebody has stolen my wallet.) Hvad så, **noget** nyt? (What is up, anything new?) Jeg mente faktisk **noget** andet. (I actually meant something else.) Vi har ikke **nogen** altan. (We do not have a balcony.) Jeg har **ingen** kontanter. (I have no cash.) Der er **intet** bedre end mormors æblekage. (Nothing is better than grandma's apple cake.)¶• In questions and after ikke, Danish uses nogen/noget, not ingen: Har du **nogen** penge? Jeg kan ikke se **noget** godt i det.¶• **Ingen** is a negative on its own, so do not add ikke: Jeg har **ingen** penge.¶• Neuter nouns take **noget/intet**: noget vand.¶• Nogle (plural) = some: nogle gange (sometimes).
B2|pronouns|Relative der and som; Det er ... der|125,154,1161,1335,2791,3760,4512,4665,4907,5691,6093|Der and som introduce relative clauses; as a subject you must keep one of them, and Det er ... der stresses a part.|A relative clause adds information to a noun. Danish uses **der** or **som**. When the relative word is the subject of its clause, you cannot leave it out; as an object, som is optional or omitted.¶Examples as subject: Er der nogen, **der** sidder her? (Is anyone sitting here?) Folk **der** holder orden, er bare for dovne til at lede. (People who keep order are lazy.) Den, **der** rejser, har noget at fortælle. (Whoever travels has something to tell.) Det er et vigtigt aspekt, **som** tit bliver overset. (It is an important aspect that is often overlooked.)¶Cleft sentences use **Det er ... der/som** to stress a part: Det er dråben, **der** får bægeret til at flyde over. (It is the last straw.) Når produktet er gratis, er det dig, **der** er produktet. (When the product is free, you are the product.)¶• After what-clauses: Det, **der** mangler, er politisk vilje. (What is missing is political will.)¶• Hvad der sker (what happens) uses der: Jeg er spændt på, hvad **der** sker.¶• Mistake: Det er dråben får bægeret ... (without der).
B2|adjectives|Comparative: -ere, mere and end|424,573,4271,4412,4815,5167,5503,5611,4824,1819|Add -ere to short adjectives, mere to long ones, and use end for than.|Compare in Danish with **-ere** on short adjectives or **mere** before long ones, and **end** for than.¶T:Adjective¦Comparative//høj¦højere//gammel¦ældre//vigtig¦vigtigere//interessant¦mere interessant//dyr¦dyrere¶Examples: Min bror er **ældre end** mig. (My brother is older than me.) Blod er **tykkere end** vand. (Blood is thicker than water.) Priserne stiger **hurtigere end** lønningerne. (Prices rise faster than wages.) Økologiske varer er **dyrere**, men bedre for miljøet. (Organic goods are more expensive but better for the environment.) Elbiler bliver **mere og mere** populære. (Electric cars are becoming more and more popular.)¶• Irregular: god – bedre – bedst; dårlig – værre – værst; mange – flere; lidt – mindre – mindst.¶• Danish says end, not som or at: **end** for different, **som** for equal: så høj **som** (as tall as).¶• The comparative does not take -t or -e: en højere mand, et højere hus, højere huse.¶• Tip: use mere ... end for -ende and -et participles: mere irriterende.
B2|adjectives|Superlative: -est, mest and the definite forms|605,1287,2159,2919,3371,3494,4633,1140,2611|Superlative: -est or mest; after den/det/de or a noun it takes -e, and best is the bare adverb form.|The superlative is made with **-st/-est** on short adjectives and **mest** before long ones. As a predicate, the bare form is often enough: Hun er **hurtigst**. With the article, it takes -e: den, det, de + **-ste**.¶Examples: Han er den **yngste** i familien. (He is the youngest in the family.) Det var det **bedste** måltid i lang tid. (That was the best meal in a long time.) Latter er den **bedste** medicin. (Laughter is the best medicine.) Det **vigtigste** er at være med. (The most important thing is taking part.) Jeg køber kun det **mest** nødvendige. (I only buy the most necessary.)¶• Irregular: god – bedre – bedst; dårlig – værre – værst; gammel – ældre – ældst; mange – flest.¶• Adverb use has no article: Hvordan kommer jeg **nemmest** ind til centrum? (What is the easiest way into the centre?) Jeg holder **mest** af te.¶• Mistake: den bedste bilen. After the superlative, the noun stays bare: den bedste bil.¶• Tip: det meste/det mindste = most/least, a very common phrase.
B2|adjectives|Noget + neuter adjective: noget sødt, noget nyt|87,128,1324,1325,1418,1484,2933,4294|After noget, intet, alt and meget, the adjective takes the neuter -t form: noget godt, noget nyt.|After indefinite pronouns, the adjective takes the **neuter -t form**, because noget, intet, alt, meget and lidt are treated as neuter.¶Examples: Jeg kunne godt tænke mig **noget sødt**. (I would like something sweet.) Jeg laver **noget let** i dag. (I am making something light today.) Det er aldrig for sent at begynde på **noget nyt**. (It is never too late to start something new.) (Nothing special.)¶T:Pronoun¦Adjective¦Example//noget¦-t¦noget godt//intet¦-t¦intet nyt//alt¦-t¦alt godt//meget¦-t¦meget interessant//lidt¦-t¦lidt sjovt¶• Adjectives in -sk and -ende/-e stay unchanged: noget dansk, noget spændende.¶• Mistake: noget sød. Danish needs the neuter -t: noget sødt.¶• Tip: this rule is why Alt godt! means all the best.
B2|adjectives|Participles as adjectives: -ende and -et/-t|956,1865,2144,2173,2688,2914,3046,3397,286,622,502|The present participle (-ende) becomes an adjective that never changes; past participles agree like adjectives.|Danish forms many adjectives from verbs. The present participle ends in **-ende** (irriterende), and does not change with gender or number. The past participle (-et, -ede, -t) can also be used as an adjective and takes the normal agreement endings.¶Examples with -ende: Skimmelsvampen er **irriterende**. (The mould is annoying.) Kvaliteten er **skuffende**. (The quality is disappointing.) Landskabet var **betagende**. (The scenery was breathtaking.) De **forsvarende** mestre er ude. (The defending champions are out.) Jeg har brug for en **smertestillende** pille. (I need a painkiller.)¶Examples with past participles: Jeg er ret **stresset**. (I am rather stressed.) Hun er helt **forelsket**. (She is head over heels in love.) Jeg er **bekymret** for min far. (I am worried about my father.)¶• Agreement: en forelsket pige, et forelsket par, forelskede mennesker.¶• Mistake: Jeg er irriterende (I am annoying) vs Jeg er irriteret (I am irritated).¶• Tip: -ende is like English -ing; -et like -ed.
B2|preps|Time prepositions: i, på, om, inden, indtil, fra|439,446,450,680,1075,1283,1664,1716,1717,1808|Choose the preposition by meaning: i for months and periods, på for days, om for parts of the day and habits, inden for deadlines.|Danish time prepositions are not the same as English ones. Learn them as small groups.¶T:Use¦Preposition¦Example//months, seasons, years¦i¦i maj, i 2024//weekdays, dates¦på¦på fredag, på lørdag//part of day, habits¦om¦om morgenen, om efteråret//deadline (by)¦inden¦inden fredag//until¦indtil, til¦indtil fredag//from¦fra¦fra mandag¶Examples: Jeg har fødselsdag **i** maj. Jeg skal have det gjort færdigt **inden** fredag. (I have to finish it by Friday.) Jeg er på ferie **indtil** fredag. (I am on holiday until Friday.) Jeg kan træffes igen **fra** mandag. (I am reachable again from Monday.)¶• Om with the part of the day usually has a definite ending: om morgenen, om aftenen. Om fem minutter means in five minutes.¶• Mistake: i fredag. A single day needs på.¶• Tip: på fredag is next or this Friday; om fredagen is every Friday.
B2|preps|Fixed prepositions after verbs and adjectives|122,484,501,694,1729,2111,3048,3463,3485,3727,3801,3701|Many verbs and adjectives take one set preposition: glæde sig til, stolt af, bange for, tænke over.|A large group of Danish verbs and adjectives is followed by one fixed preposition. It often differs from English, so learn them as a chunk.¶T:Chunk¦Meaning//glæde sig til¦look forward to//stolt af¦proud of//bange for¦afraid of//sur på¦cross with//tænke over¦think about (reflect)//interessere sig for¦be interested in//afhænge af¦depend on//god til¦good at¶Examples: Jeg glæder mig **til** familiefesten. (I am looking forward to the family party.) Jeg er stolt **af** dig. (I am proud of you.) Jeg er bange **for** nåle. (I am afraid of needles.) Jeg er ikke sur **på** dig. (I am not cross with you.) Det afhænger **af** det. (That depends.) Jeg interesserer mig ikke **for** sport. (I am not interested in sport.)¶• Some verbs change meaning with the preposition: tænke på (think of, remember) vs tænke over (consider).¶• Before a verb the preposition takes at: Jeg er bange for **at** være alene. (I am afraid of being alone.)¶• Tip: keep a list and always learn the preposition with the word.
B2|preps|Compound prepositions: på grund af, i stedet for|992,1146,2646,3086,3584,3587,3874,4269,5148,6323|Multi-word prepositions such as på grund af, i stedet for and med hensyn til are fixed phrases.|Danish often uses prepositions built from several words. They are fixed and are common in formal speech and writing.¶T:Phrase¦Meaning//på grund af¦because of//i stedet for¦instead of//ved siden af¦next to / on the side//i forhold til¦in relation to, compared to//med hensyn til¦regarding//inden for¦within//uden for¦outside//på trods af¦in spite of//ifølge¦according to¶Examples: **På grund af** en signalfejl er kørslen forsinket. (Due to a signal fault, the journey is delayed.) Jeg får den repareret **i stedet for** at smide den ud. (I am having it repaired instead of throwing it away.) Jeg er optimistisk **med hensyn til** fremtiden. (I am optimistic about the future.) Vi halter bagud **i forhold til** tidsplanen. (We are behind schedule.) Recepten skal indløses **inden for** 28 dage. (The prescription must be filled within 28 days.) Han blev frifundet **på grund af** manglende beviser. (He was acquitted because of lack of evidence.)¶• Before a verb, add at: i stedet for **at** smide ud. (Without at, it is a mistake.)¶• Note the spelling: **inden for** and **uden for** are written as two words when they are prepositions.¶• Tip: på grund af is neutral; in writing it is often abbreviated pga.
B2|conj|Da, når and mens (time clauses)|113,1006,1080,2221,2748,2896,3016,3479,4103,4350|Da = once in the past; når = whenever or in the future; mens = during.|English uses when for both; Danish splits it.¶T:Conjunction¦Use¦Example//**da**¦one single event in the past¦da budet kom (when the courier came)//**når**¦present, future or repeated¦når du går ud (when you leave)//**mens**¦at the same time as¦mens jeg er væk (while I am away)¶Examples with da: Jeg brækkede armen, **da** jeg stod på ski. (I broke my arm when I was skiing.) Den var allerede i stykker, **da** jeg købte den. (It was already broken when I bought it.) Jeg var ikke hjemme, **da** budet kom. (I was not home when the courier came.)¶Examples with når: Sluk lyset, **når** du går ud. (Turn off the light when you leave.) Jeg får tit hovedpine, **når** jeg er stresset. (I often get headaches when I am stressed.) **Når** jeg får lejlighed, kontakter jeg dig. (When I get the chance, I will contact you.)¶Examples with mens: Kan du vande blomsterne, **mens** jeg er væk? (Can you water the flowers while I am away?) **Mens** du laver mad, dækker jeg bord. (While you cook, I will set the table.)¶• Repeated past action uses når too: Når jeg var ung, spillede jeg fodbold. (Whenever I was young...)¶• Mistake: da jeg går ud (present). Da is only for the past.
B2|conj|Concession and condition: selvom, hvis, medmindre, som om|178,368,1969,2694,3006,3570,4319,6116,6119|Selvom = even though; hvis = if; medmindre = unless; som om = as if.|These conjunctions start subordinate clauses with the verb after the subject (subject, adverb, verb).¶T:Conjunction¦Meaning¦Example//selvom¦although¦selvom jeg lige er kommet hjem//hvis¦if¦hvis den ikke passer//medmindre¦unless¦medmindre vi finder en bedre løsning//som om¦as if¦som om jeg har været gennem kødhakkeren¶Examples: Jeg har allerede udlængsel, **selvom** jeg lige er kommet hjem. (I already have wanderlust although I have just got home.) Kan jeg levere den tilbage, **hvis** den ikke passer? (Can I return it if it does not fit?) Sig til, **hvis** der ændrer sig noget. (Let me know if anything changes.) **Medmindre** du har en bedre idé. (Unless you have a better idea.) Jeg føler mig, **som om** jeg har været gennem kødhakkeren. (I feel as if I have been through the wringer.)¶• **Som var det ...** is a literary alternative to som om: Man bør leve hver dag, som var det den sidste. (You should live every day as if it were the last.)¶• The condition clause can also come second: Jeg kommer, hvis du har tid. For whether in indirect questions use om: Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer.¶• A subordinate clause that comes first causes inversion in the main clause: Hvis du har tid, kommer jeg.¶• Spelling: selvom is normally written as one word (selv om is also accepted).
B2|conj|Paired conjunctions: både ... og, hverken ... eller|595,4679,5747,5990,6111,6112,6113,6114,5515,1396|Both ... and, neither ... nor, not only ... but also and the more ... the more.|Paired conjunctions link two parts of equal rank.¶T:Pair¦Meaning//både ... og¦both ... and//hverken ... eller¦neither ... nor//enten ... eller¦either ... or//ikke kun ... men også¦not only ... but also//jo ... desto / jo ... jo¦the more ... the more¶Examples: Vi deler **både** glæder **og** sorger. (I feel foreign both here and there.) **Hverken** den ene **eller** den anden løsning er perfekt. (Neither the one nor the other solution is perfect.) **Ikke kun** omkostningerne, **men også** arbejdet er enormt. (Not only the cost but also the work is enormous.) **Jo** længere vi venter, **desto** dyrere bliver det. (The longer we wait, the more expensive it gets.) **Jo** mere vi ved, **desto** mere indser vi, hvad vi ikke ved.¶• After hverken ... eller there is no extra negative: Jeg ved hverken ud eller ind. (I am at a complete loss.)¶• Both parts must be of the same kind: både i dag og i morgen.¶• Tip: jo ... jo and jo ... desto both work; desto is more formal.
B2|conj|Purpose and manner: for at, uden at, i stedet for at|2269,2304,2715,2717,3072,3086,3095|For at = in order to; uden at = without; i stedet for at = instead of: all take an infinitive.|These fixed phrases are followed by **at** + infinitive.¶T:Phrase¦Meaning¦Example//for at¦in order to¦for at bevare overblikket//uden at¦without¦uden at gøre væsen af sig//i stedet for at¦instead of¦i stedet for at smide ud//efter at¦after (formal)¦efter at have spist¶Examples: Jeg dyrker sport **for at** få hovedet på plads. B2|conj|At-clauses after adjectives and verbs (glad for, at)|3270,3681,3700,3730,3808,3813,3814,3882,6083|At introduces a that-clause after verbs and adjectives: glad for, at; synes, at; mener, at.|**At** (that) introduces a subordinate clause. B2|conj|Linking adverbs: altså, alligevel, derfor, dermed|146,147,168,326,334,4741,4891,6058,6130,6142|Adverbs like altså, alligevel, derfor, dog and dermed connect ideas and trigger inversion when they start a sentence.|Linking adverbs show how two sentences relate. B2|neg|Negative words: ingen, intet, ingenting, aldrig|331,569,718,766,783,916,997,1517,2839|Ingen, intet, ingenting and aldrig are negative in themselves: do not add ikke.|Danish has a set of negative words that already carry the negation. B2|neg|Fine negation: ikke længere, næsten ikke, slet ikke|322,1013,1396,3987,4256,4425,5644,1400|Ikke mere/længere, næsten ikke, slet ikke, hverken ... eller and på ingen måde grade the negation.|Besides plain ikke, Danish has many ways to grade or sharpen a negation.¶T:Phrase¦Meaning//ikke længere / ikke mere¦no longer, not any more//næsten ikke / knap¦hardly//slet ikke¦not at all//på ingen måde¦by no means//ikke noget¦not anything (also nothing for me)//hverken ... eller¦neither ... nor¶Examples: Lyset i gangen virker **ikke mere**. Jeg ved hverken ud eller ind.

(You are joking, are you not?) Jeg forstyrrer **vel ikke**? (I am not disturbing you, am I?) Vi kender vist ikke hinanden**, vel**? (We have not met, have we?) Så det vil sige, du kommer **ikke**? (So that means you are not coming?) Forstår jeg dig ret, at du ikke kommer? (Do I understand correctly that you are not coming?)¶• Danish tags do not change with the verb or person, unlike English isn't it / don't you.¶• A rising intonation turns a statement into a question: Du kommer?¶• Vel inside the sentence softens a question: Det er vel ikke et problem?¶• Tip: Ikke? is the safest all-purpose tag.
B2|mood|S-passive with modal verbs and in the infinitive|1905,2954,3296,3446,3501,3587,3593,4183,4302|Add -s to the infinitive after skal, kan, må, bør to make a passive: skal opereres, kan forhandles.|The Danish s-passive is formed by adding **-s** to the verb. It is most common in the infinitive after a modal, and in the present for general facts.¶T:Active infinitive¦S-passive//forhandle¦forhandles//operere¦opereres//justere¦justeres//udskyde¦udskydes¶Examples: Prisen kan **forhandles**. (The price can be negotiated.) Jeg skal **opereres**. (I need to be operated on.) Såret skal **sys**. (The wound needs stitches.) Dosis skal **justeres**. (The dose needs adjusting.) Sygdommen er kronisk, men kan **behandles**. (The illness is chronic but can be treated.) Det kan ikke **udskydes** længere. (That cannot be put off any longer.) Det skal **indsendes** inden fristen. (It must be submitted by the deadline.)¶• Verbs ending in -e add -s: forhandle, forhandles. Verbs ending in a consonant (not -e) add -es: sys, but sende, sendes.¶• The s-passive describes a general process; for a specific event use blive + participle (see next rule).¶• The agent can be added with af: Det skal besluttes **af** ledelsen.¶• Mistake: Prisen kan forhandle. A passive needs the -s.
B2|mood|Blive-passive: blev, bliver, er blevet + participle|1811,1976,1999,2242,2296,2607,4652,4771,5311|Blive + participle is the passive for single events; the agent is introduced with af.|The blive-passive uses **blive** + past participle. It stresses an event or a change and is the most common passive in the past tense.¶T:Tense¦Form¦Example//present¦bliver + participle¦Mange opgaver bliver automatiseret.//past¦blev + participle¦Han blev udelukket i to år.//perfect¦er blevet + participle¦Flyet er blevet aflyst.¶Examples: Han **blev udvist** for at stoppe en klar scoringschance. (He was sent off for stopping a clear scoring chance.) Mødet **er blevet flyttet** til torsdag. (The meeting has been moved to Thursday.) Kommentarfunktionen **blev slået** fra. (The comment function was switched off.) Opkøbet **blev forbudt** af konkurrencemyndighederne. (The takeover was blocked by the competition authority.)¶• **Af** introduces the agent: Sagen blev malket **af** medierne. (The case was exploited by the media.)¶• The participle agrees in the passive only when it is used as an adjective; after blive it is often the plain -et/-t form: Børnene blev passet.¶• In the perfect, the participle follows blevet: Hun er blevet forfremmet til afdelingsleder.¶• Mistake: Mødet er flyttet if you mean the event happened. That describes the result, not the action.
B2|mood|Imperative: commands, requests and lad os|76,89,112,133,152,270,477,810,1010,1080|The imperative is the verb stem; add lige, bare or venligst to soften; lad os means let us.|The Danish imperative is the **stem** of the verb (the infinitive without -e): **Kom!**, **Vent!**, **Tag!**. There is no separate plural form.¶Examples: **Vent** lige lidt! (Wait a moment!) **Pas** godt på dig selv! (Take care of yourself!) **Kom** ind! (Come in!) **Kom** godt hjem! (Get home safely!) **Tag** din kæreste med! (Bring your boyfriend along!) **Sluk** lyset, når du går ud. (Turn off the light when you leave.) **Tag** dig ikke af det. (Do not let it bother you.)¶To be more polite use **lige** or **bare**: **Tag lige** skoene af. (Please take your shoes off.) **Sæt bare** tasken der. (Just put the bag there.) Or use a question: Kan du ...? / Vil du ikke lige ...?¶• **Lad os** + infinitive = let us: Lad os holde kontakten. Lad mig tale færdig!¶• Negative imperative: put ikke after the verb: Glem ikke at ringe.¶• Verbs ending in -e lose the e: tage, tag; vente, vent; sidde, sid. Some end in -r or -d: bære, bær.¶• Tip: tone matters. Commands without lige or tak can sound blunt.
B2|mood|Wishes and unreal conditions: ville ønske, hvis jeg bare|3664,4325,4326,925,5872,2535,228,3480|Use past tense (havde, kunne) or ville + infinitive for unreal situations; jeg ville ønske for wishes.|Danish expresses wishes and unreal conditions with the **past tense**, which has a hypothetical meaning, and with **ville** for the result.¶T:Idea¦Pattern//wish (present)¦Jeg ville ønske, (at) jeg havde ...//wish (past)¦Jeg ville ønske, (at) jeg havde haft ...//unreal if¦Hvis jeg kunne ..., ville jeg ...//result¦ville + infinitive¶Examples: Jeg **ville ønske**, jeg **havde** mere tid. (That would be really sweet.)¶• Add bare to show a strong wish: Hvis jeg bare havde. Or use gid: Gid jeg havde mere tid. (I wish I had more time.)¶• The past perfect is used for the unreal past: Hvis jeg havde vidst det, ville jeg være kommet.¶• Mistake: Hvis jeg vil have tid, ... Do not use ville in the if-clause.
B2|mood|State passive: er + participle vs blive|1035,1116,1676,2054,2467,2494,2836,3033,3491,2607|Er + participle describes a state; blive + participle describes the event: Butikken er lukket vs Butikken bliver lukket.|Danish distinguishes an event from the resulting state.¶T:Event (blive)¦State (være)//Butikken bliver lukket.¦Butikken er lukket.//Mødet blev aflyst.¦Mødet er aflyst.//Flyet bliver forsinket.¦Flyet er forsinket.¶The participle works like an adjective: it can take the neuter -t or the plural -e (see the rule on participles as adjectives).¶Examples of the state: Butikken **er lukket**. (It is covered by the warranty.)¶Compare the event: Flyet **er blevet** aflyst. (The flight has been cancelled.)¶• English is cancelled is both; Danish chooses.¶• Tip: use være for how it is now; use blive for what happens.
B2|numbers|Telling time: klokken, halv and kvart|4001,4003,4004,4005,4122,4214,807,1039,2931,4228,1479|Halv means half BEFORE the hour (halv fire = 3:30); kvart over and kvart i give quarter past and quarter to.|Ask Hvad er klokken? and answer **Klokken er ...**. B2|particles|Jo and da: it is obvious, of course|283,384,1445,105,312,358,487,1599,3890|Jo marks something as obvious or shared; da shows surprise or contradiction. Both are unstressed in speech.|Particles give a sentence a tone without changing its meaning. **Jo** and **da** are very common.¶• **Jo** = as you know, of course. It treats the information as known: Man må **jo** videre. (You have to keep going, you know.) Det dufter **jo** himmelsk! (It smells heavenly, doesn't it!) Nå, det var **jo** bare dejligt! (Well, that is just lovely! [ironic])¶• **Da** = of course, surely; it expresses surprise, disagreement or warmth: Det er **da** interessant! (But that is interesting!) Det er **da** sødt af dig! (That is so sweet of you!) Det er **da** noget vrøvl! (That is nonsense!) Det var **da** en selvfølge. (That was only natural.)¶• Both are placed after the verb in main clauses (and before it in subordinate clauses): Det er jo rigtigt. ... fordi det jo er rigtigt.¶• Do not confuse with the conjunction da (when) or the question word: Det er da ikke sandt?¶• Tip: jo and da cannot be translated word for word; learn them as the tone of the sentence.
B2|particles|Nok, vel and vist: probably, I suppose, apparently|271,3348,6391,3960,3152,116,202,235,323|Nok means probably or will surely; vel asks for confirmation; vist means it seems.|These small words show the speaker's attitude.¶T:Particle¦Meaning//nok¦probably; will surely (with skal)//vel¦I suppose, surely; asks for agreement//vist¦apparently, I think//skal nok¦will certainly (reassurance)¶Examples: Mine forventninger var **nok** for høje. (My expectations were probably too high.) Det skal **nok** gå. (It will be fine.) Det skal **nok** gå alt sammen. (It will all be fine.) Der kan vi **nok** godt finde ud af noget. (We can probably work something out there.) Jeg forstyrrer **vel** ikke? (I am not disturbing, am I?) Vi kender **vist** ikke hinanden, vel? (I do not think we have met, have we?) Så har vi **vist** misforstået hinanden. (So we seem to have misunderstood each other.) Jeg har **vist** udtrykt mig uklart. (I seem to have expressed myself unclearly.)¶• **Skal nok** is a reassurance: Det skal nok gå. = It will be okay, don't worry.¶• Nok also means enough: Det er ikke nok. Context shows which meaning.¶• Vist (apparently) is different from vist (shown, from vise): Det har vist sit værd.¶• Position: after the finite verb in main clauses.
B2|particles|Lige and bare: small softeners|50,96,151,209,261,804,853,94,920,1012|Lige makes a request or action casual and quick; bare means just, only, and softens commands.|**Lige** and **bare** are among the most frequent Danish particles. (I just have a question.) Må jeg **lige** skyde noget ind? (May I quickly add something?) Tænd **lige** lyset. (Turn on the light, please.) Tag **lige** af bordet. (Clear the table, please.) B2|punct|Commas: before subordinate clauses and men|159,286,653,1714,2694,3016,3270,3697,4256,4614|Put a comma before a subordinate clause and before men; after a fronted subordinate clause too.|Since the 2010 reform Danish uses grammatical commas mostly to separate clauses.¶• **Before a subordinate clause** (at, fordi, hvis, når, da, som, mens, selvom): Lægen siger**,** at jeg skal hvile mig. (The doctor says that I should rest.) Det generer mig**,** at han altid kommer for sent. (It bothers me that he is always late.)¶• **After a fronted subordinate clause**: **Hvis** du har spørgsmål**,** står jeg gerne til rådighed. (If you have any questions, I am happy to help.)¶• **Before men** when it links two clauses: Jeg er ret stresset**,** men ellers godt. (I am pretty stressed, but otherwise fine.) B2|style|Du and De: informal and formal address|231,232,233,1291,1405,49,1256|Danes use du almost everywhere; De is rare and formal, and people usually agree to say du.|In modern Danish **du** is the normal form of address, even with strangers, bosses and older people. B2|style|Signposting a talk or text (kort sagt, med andre ord)|146,147,182,183,238,239,251,333,1736|Phrases like kort sagt, med andre ord and for at vende tilbage til structure speech and writing.|Signposting phrases tell the listener where you are in your argument. B2|style|Reporting opinions: mener, siger, efter sigende|3882,3556,4919,5269,2367,3270,3952,4398|Report what others think with mener, at; siger, at or efter sigende; the verb of saying can follow the quote.|To report what someone thinks or says, Danish uses an at-clause (indirect speech) or a quote with the verb after it.¶T:Pattern¦Example//mener, at¦Mange mener, at indenrigsflyvninger burde forbydes.//siger, at¦Lægen siger, at jeg skal hvile mig.//efter sigende¦Sport er mord, sagde Churchill efter sigende.//quote + sagde¦I morgen er der også en dag, sagde hun roligt.¶Examples: Mange **mener, at** indenrigsflyvninger burde forbydes. (I think we should wait.) Lægen **siger, at** jeg skal hvile mig. (The doctor says I should rest.) Min mavefornemmelse **siger mig, at** der er noget lusk. (My gut tells me something is fishy.) Sport er mord, **sagde** Churchill **efter sigende**. (Sport is murder, Churchill is said to have said.)¶• In reported speech the verb often moves back in tense: Hun sagde, at hun var træt.¶• With a direct quote the verb of saying follows with inversion: »Det er sent«, sagde han.¶• Efter sigende / angiveligt = allegedly.
C1|tenses|Pluperfect: havde/var + participle|249,360,3715,3961,3981,4343,790,4325,4108|Havde + participle (or var with some motion verbs) looks back from a past moment; it also builds unreal pasts.|The pluperfect (**havde** + past participle) places an event before another point in the past. At C1 you meet it in narrative, in reactions and in hypothetical statements.¶• Sequence: **Åh, det havde jeg nær glemt!** (Oh, I almost forgot!)¶• Expectation: **Jeg havde forventet mig mere.** (I had expected more.)¶• Disbelief, with the object fronted: **Det havde jeg ikke troet, du kunne.** (I would not have thought you had it in you.) **Det havde jeg aldrig troet var muligt.**¶• Unreal past: **Jeg havde aldrig troet, at det ville ske.** (I never would have thought that would happen.) **Hvis jeg bare havde vidst det noget før!** (If only I had known that sooner!) **Uden ham havde jeg været på den.** (I would have been lost without him.)¶• With **var** for verbs of motion and change: **Det var tæt på, at vi var kommet for sent til flyet.** (We came within a whisker of being late.)¶Do not confuse it with the simple past of **have** (to have): **Da jeg var lille, havde jeg en hund.** (When I was little, I had a dog.) has no participle.¶Tip for English speakers: Danish often uses **havde** where English says "would have" in unreal conditions (**havde jeg vidst det**). Keep the adverb after havde: **Det havde jeg aldrig troet.**
C1|tenses|Future: kommer til at, vil, skal and the present|2767,3186,6031,3954,6355,271,3348,4970,525,3471|Kommer til at predicts; skal and vil carry plans and will; the present with a time word often does the job.|Danish has no real future tense. It uses several options with different shades.¶• **Komme til at** + infinitive is the most neutral prediction: **Det kommer til at koste mig en mindre formue.** (That is going to cost me a small fortune.) **Det kommer til at gå over i historiebøgerne.**¶• **Skal** = plan, promise or reassurance: **Jeg skal helt sikkert stemme.** (I am definitely going to vote.) **Det skal nok gå.** (It will be fine.)¶• **Vil** = will, often formal or predictive: **Din henvendelse vil blive behandlet hurtigst muligt.** (Your request will be processed as quickly as possible.) **Jeg kan ikke ryste følelsen af mig, at der vil ske noget.**¶• Present tense with a time word: **Jeg bliver udskrevet i morgen.** (I am being discharged tomorrow.) **Han bliver far i næste måned.**¶Negatives: **Jeg kommer aldrig til at glemme dig.** The adverb sits between kommer and til.¶Tip: unlike modals, **kommer til at** needs the infinitive marker **at**. Note that **blive** also gives a future of becoming: **Det bliver svært.** (It will be hard.)
C1|tenses|Perfect with siden and duration|491,701,762,1939,3400,3848,456,1668,5716,3340|Danish uses har + participle with siden or i X tid for situations that began in the past and still hold.|Where English has "have been -ing", Danish uses the plain **perfect** with a time expression.¶• **Siden** (since): **Vi har kendt hinanden siden skoletiden.** (We have known each other since school.) **Jeg har haft ondt i halsen siden i går.** **Jeg har været i godt humør, siden jeg vågnede.**¶• **I + period** (for): **Jeg har arbejdet her i tre år.** (I have been working here for three years.) **Vi har været sammen i fem år.** **Jeg har skrantet i flere uger.**¶• With a clause after siden: **De to har været som ler og langhalm, siden de var små.** (The two have been inseparable since they were little.) **Jeg har spillet klaver, siden jeg var barn.**¶• **Har kun gjort ... siden**: **Hun har kun gjort det mest nødvendige siden omstruktureringen.**¶The clause after siden is in the past tense, but the main clause is in the perfect.¶Mistake: using the present tense like many languages do (Jeg arbejder her i tre år). That sounds like a plan for the future.¶Tip: no ongoing form is needed, so har arbejdet covers both "have worked" and "have been working".
C1|tenses|Preterite or perfect: finished vs. relevant|457,678,2065,5874,5729,3016,4837,4385,5716,6218|Use the preterite for a finished event at a known time; use the perfect when the time is open or still relevant.|Danish distinguishes the **preterite** (præteritum) and the **perfect** (perfektum) much as English does, but it is a little stricter.¶• **Preterite** = a finished event in a definite past time (yesterday, last year, in 1989): **Vi blev gift sidste år.** (We got married last year.) **Han døde sidste år.** **Jeg løb ti kilometer i går.** **Muren faldt i november 1989.** **Domkirken blev bygget i middelalderen.**¶• **Preterite** also for the situation during a told event: **Jeg var ikke hjemme, da budet kom.** (I was not at home when the courier came.)¶• **Perfect** = the past is connected to now, or no time is given: **Vi har tøvet for længe.** (We have hesitated too long.) **Sådan har vi altid fejret det.** (We have always celebrated like this.) **Jeg har kæmpet længe med mig selv.**¶• With **siden**, the perfect continues until now: **Jeg har spillet klaver, siden jeg var barn.**¶Mistake: using the perfect with a definite time word, as people sometimes do in English speech. **I går har jeg løbet** is wrong; say **I går løb jeg**.¶Tip: ask yourself whether the time is a completed point. If so, use the preterite.
C1|tenses|Being in the middle of it: være ved at, lige ved at|2282,5530,1872,3053,5657,3922,3914,2786,3385,1528|Være ved at expresses an action in progress or about to happen; lige ved at means nearly.|Danish has no "-ing" form. **Være ved at** + infinitive covers two meanings.¶• Action in progress: **Jeg er ved at lære at surfe.** (I am learning to surf.) **Jeg er ved at skrive min bacheloropgave.** (I am writing my thesis.) **Jeg er ved at omskole mig.** (I am retraining.)¶• Gradual change: **Bymidten er ved at uddø.** (The city center is dying out.) **Mange dialekter er ved at uddø.**¶• About to happen, with emphasis: **Jeg er ved at sprænges af stolthed.** (I am bursting with pride.) **Jeg er ved at dø af sult.** (I am ravenous.)¶• **Lige ved at** = on the point of, almost: **Vi var lige ved at misse færgen.** (We very nearly missed the ferry.) **Jeg er lige ved at besvime.** (I am about to keel over.)¶• Past: **Jeg var ved at dø af skræk.** (I nearly died of fright.)¶Also common in spoken Danish: posture verbs with **og**, such as **sidde og læse** (be sitting reading), **stå og vente** (be standing waiting), **ligge og sove**. Compare **Det står og falder med budgettet.** (It stands and falls with the budget.)¶Mistake: **Jeg er læsende**. Use **Jeg er ved at læse**.
C1|order|Fronting the object: Det havde jeg ikke troet|195,360,3981,249,785,1492,126,3948|Placing the object first for emphasis keeps the verb in second place; the subject follows the verb.|Danish is a **verb-second (V2)** language: the finite verb is always the second element in a main clause. You can put almost anything first, even the object, but the subject then moves after the verb.¶T:Order¦Example//Subject first¦Jeg havde ikke troet det.//Object first¦Det havde jeg ikke troet.¶• **Det havde jeg ikke troet, du kunne.** (I would not have thought you had it in you.) The object **det** is fronted for emphasis.¶• **Det havde jeg slet ikke på radaren.** (That was not on my radar.) **Det fik jeg ikke med.** (I did not catch that.)¶• With a modal: **Det kan man trygt spise endnu.** (You can still eat that without worry.) **Tillid må man gøre sig fortjent til.** (Trust has to be earned.) **Det skal jeg lige have fordøjet.**¶• **Åh, det havde jeg nær glemt!** (Oh, I almost forgot!)¶Fronting links your sentence to what was just said and adds emphasis or contrast.¶Mistake: keeping the English order (**Det jeg havde ikke troet**). The verb must stay second.¶Tip: fronted **det** often replaces a whole earlier idea. Use it freely in speech.
C1|order|Subordinate clause first: then verb before subject|314,4106,4108,136,177,300|When a subordinate clause opens the sentence, the main clause that follows starts with its verb.|A fronted subordinate clause counts as the first element, so the verb of the main clause comes next. The subject follows the verb.¶T:Subordinate clause¦Verb¦Subject//Hvis du tillader,¦vil¦jeg gerne tilføje noget.//Da jeg var lille,¦havde¦jeg en hund.¶• **Hvis du tillader, vil jeg gerne tilføje noget.** (If you will allow me, I would like to add something.)¶• **Hvis jeg ikke tager fejl, har vi mødt hinanden før.** (If I am not mistaken, we have met before.) **Hvis jeg husker rigtigt, mødte vi hinanden i Wien.**¶• **Hvis jeg skal være ærlig, havde jeg mine tvivl.** (If I am honest, I had doubts.)¶• **Da jeg var lille, havde jeg en hund.** (When I was little, I had a dog.) **Siden jeg flyttede hertil, har jeg været glad.**¶• Comma: put a comma after the fronted clause. Word order inside the clause is normal: subject, adverb, verb.¶Mistake: **Hvis du tillader, jeg vil gerne** (subject before the verb). In Danish the verb must come right after the comma.¶Tip: this is the same rule as for **Nu**, **I dag** or **Derfor** at the start: whatever stands first, the verb is second.
C1|order|Sentence adverbs in subordinate clauses|208,236,1085,1103,2758,3006,3697,4247,4256,6335|In subordinate clauses sentence adverbs such as ikke, aldrig and allerede stand before the finite verb.|In a **main clause** the adverb follows the verb: **Han kommer ikke.** In a **subordinate clause** the adverb stands **before** the finite verb: **at han ikke kommer.**¶T:Main clause¦Subordinate clause//Du kommer ikke.¦..., at du ikke kommer.//Det er aldrig rent.¦..., at det aldrig er rent.¶• **Det er ærgerligt, at du ikke kommer.** (It is a shame that you are not coming.) **Forstår jeg dig ret, at du ikke kommer?**¶• **Jeg har en fornemmelse af, at lejligheden aldrig er ren.** (I feel like the apartment is never clean.)¶• **Jeg trådte i spinaten, fordi jeg ikke kendte skikkene.** (I put my foot in it because I did not know the customs.) **Jeg er sent på den, fordi bussen ikke kom.**¶• **Hvad laver du, når du ikke arbejder?** **Kan jeg levere den tilbage, hvis den ikke passer?**¶• **Jeg kan næsten ikke tro, at det allerede er december.** (I can hardly believe it is already December.)¶Other adverbs behave the same: **også, altid, aldrig, allerede, stadig, bare, nok**.¶Tip: with a compound tense, the adverb still comes before the auxiliary: **fordi jeg ikke har set den**. C1|verbs|Wishes and polite wishes: ville ønske, hvis bare, ville gerne|3664,925,512,932,1970,228,3480,6348,4325,4367|Jeg ville ønske plus past tense expresses a wish; hvis bare + havde marks regret; ville gerne is a polite want.|Danish expresses wishes and regrets with the past tense and with **ville**.¶• **Jeg ville ønske, (at) jeg havde ...** (I wish I had ...): **Jeg ville ønske, jeg havde mere tid.** (I wish I had more time.) C1|verbs|Reflexive verbs with sig|371,484,1526,1936,2111,2772,3657,3862,3574,1165|Many verbs need sig/mig/dig/os; some exist only as reflexives (glæde sig, skamme sig, føle sig).|Danish reflexive verbs take **mig, dig, sig, os, jer, sig** (sig for the third person, singular and plural).¶T:Person¦Pronoun¦Example//jeg¦mig¦**Jeg skammer mig.**//du¦dig¦**Du føler dig ensom.**//han/hun/de¦sig¦**Han interesserer sig for sport.**//vi¦os¦**Vi forkæler os selv.**¶• Only reflexive: **Jeg glæder mig til at ses igen snart.** (I look forward to seeing you again soon.) **Jeg skammer mig over min opførsel.** (I am ashamed of my behavior.)¶• **Føle sig** + adjective: **Jeg føler mig ikke værdsat.** (I do not feel valued.) **Jeg føler mig som et nyt menneske.**¶• Meaning changes: **Jeg interesserer mig ikke for sport.** (I am not interested in sports.) C1|verbs|Lade sig + infinitive|568,706,1859,1962,2346,5029,5423,191|Lade sig expresses allowing, resisting or being able to be done; it often has a passive feel.|**Lade sig** + infinitive has a reflexive form, but the meaning is passive: the subject is influenced, not acting.¶• Allowing: **Jeg lader mig gerne belære.** (I am happy to be proven wrong.) **Han lader sig kommandere rundt med af hende.** (He lets her boss him around.)¶• Resisting, with a negative: **Han lader sig ikke sige noget.** (He will not listen to anyone.) **Han lader sig ikke slå ud.** (He does not let himself be beaten.)¶• Politics: **Politikerne må ikke lade sig styre af interessegrupper.** (Politicians mustn't let themselves be steered by interest groups.)¶• **Lade sig vaccinere** (to get vaccinated), **lade sig skille** (to get a divorce).¶• Fixed phrase **lade sig gøre** (be feasible): **Det kan ikke lade sig gøre.** (That is not feasible.) **Det kan godt lade sig gøre.** (That can be arranged.)¶The agent is added with **af**. C1|modal|Modal + have/være + participle: past modality|1769,2138,4323,790,4325,4343|Kunne, ville and burde + have + participle describe missed or hypothetical past actions.|To talk about what could, should or would have happened, put the modal in the right form and add **have** or **være** with a participle.¶• **kunne have** (could have): **Mødet kunne have været en mail.** (The meeting could have been an email.) **Kampen kunne næsten ikke have været mere spændende.** (The game could hardly have been more exciting.)¶• **ville have** (would have): **Set tilbage ville jeg have gjort meget anderledes.** (Looking back, I would do a lot differently.)¶• **burde have** (should have): **Jeg burde have ringet.** (I should have called.)¶• **skulle have**: **Du skulle have sagt det.** (You should have said it.)¶Only the modal is conjugated; **have** stays in the infinitive. C1|articles|Den/det/de + adjective: no suffix on the noun|201,343,739,1060,1097,1157,1287,1406,1555|With a preposed den/det/de and an adjective, the noun stays bare: den gamle ejendom, not den gamle ejendommen.|When a definite noun has an adjective, Danish marks definiteness **once**, with a free article (**den, det, de**) in front of the adjective. C1|articles|Indefinite article in judgments: Det er en fornøjelse|180,301,328,359,593,1131,1342,1371,1709,1793|After det er/var, Danish uses en/et before the noun in comments and judgments, much like English a/an.|With **Det er/var + noun**, Danish puts the indefinite article in front of the noun when you comment on or judge something.¶• Polite phrases: **Det er en fornøjelse at møde dig.** (It is a pleasure to meet you.) **Det er en nydelse.** (That is a real treat.)¶• Judgments: **Det var en fiasko.** (That was a flop.) **Det var en misforståelse.** (That was a misunderstanding.) **Det er en smagssag.** (That is a matter of taste.)¶• Idioms: **Det er en helt anden sag.** (That is a different story.) **Det er en dråbe i havet.** (That is a drop in the ocean.) **Det er en saga blot.** (That is water under the bridge.)¶• Ironic: **Nå, det var en køn historie!** (Well, that is a fine mess!)¶Contrast: with a plain profession or nationality the article is dropped: **Hun er lærer. Han er dansker.** Once an adjective or a characterising phrase is added, the article returns: **Hun er en god lærer.**¶Mistake: leaving out **en/et** in sentences like Det er fornøjelse. It sounds telegraphic. The gender follows the noun: **et problem, en sag**.
C1|nouns|Irregular and unchanged plurals|403,410,409,54,357,669,582,504,725,1045|Danish has many irregular plurals: et barn becomes børn, en mand becomes mænd; some nouns, like år and ting, do not change.|Most Danish plurals add **-er**, **-e** or **-r**, but a core group of very common nouns breaks the pattern.¶T:Singular¦Plural¦Note//et barn¦børn¦vowel change, no ending//en bror¦brødre¦vowel change//en tand¦tænder¦vowel change//en hånd¦hænder¦vowel change//et øje¦øjne¦ending -er dropped//et år¦år¦unchanged//en ting¦ting¦unchanged¶• **Vi har to børn.** (We have two children.) **Har du børn?** (Do you have children?) **Jeg har to brødre.** (I have two brothers.)¶• Body parts: **Jeg børster tænder.** (I brush my teeth.) **Han er god med sine hænder.** (He is good with his hands.) **Jeg tror ikke mine egne ører.** (I can not believe my ears.)¶• Unchanged: **Min datter er fem år gammel.** (five years old) **Vi laver mange ting sammen.**¶The definite plural adds -ene/-ne to the plural: **børnene, tænderne, årene, tingene**.¶Mistake: **barner**, **tander**.
