C1|nouns|The genitive -s (no apostrophe)|697,704,771,1251,1481,1818,1887,1977,2793,6198,550,1333|Possession is shown with -s added to the owner, without an apostrophe: mors øjne, familiens problembarn.|Danish has no case system, but a possessor takes the ending **-s**, and the owner comes before the thing owned, as in English. There is **no apostrophe**.¶• **Hun har sin mors øjne.** (She has her mother's eyes.) **Han er familiens problembarn.** (He is the family's problem child.)¶• With definite owners: **mandens hjerte** (the man's heart), **chefens højre hånd**, **landets skikke**, **sagens kerne**, **husets regning**.¶• Set phrases: **dagens ret** (dish of the day), **dagens vigtigste måltid** (the most important meal of the day).¶• With plural measures: **seks måneders prøvetid** (a six-month probation period), **tre måneders opsigelse**.¶• The apostrophe appears only after a name ending in -s, -x or -z: **Hans' bil**, **Thomas' hus**.¶The -s attaches to the last word of a phrase: **min kollegas bil**, **Jens og Maries hus**.¶Mistake: **Peter's bil**, the English style. Danish writes **Peters bil**.¶Tip: for things, a prepositional phrase is often better: **kapitlet i bogen** rather than bogens kapitel.
C1|pronouns|Generic man (and en, ens)|47,281,283,393,785,1120,1167,1175,1378,2696|Man means one/you in general; it is subject-only. The object form is en and the possessive is ens.|**Man** is the impersonal pronoun meaning "one", "you" or "people in general". It is used only as a **subject** and takes a normal verb.¶• **Man gør, hvad man kan.** (You do what you can.) **Man må jo videre.** (You have to keep going.)¶• **I byen er man mere anonym.** (You are more anonymous in the city.)¶• With a modal: **Man kunne spise direkte fra gulvet.** (You could eat off the floor.)¶• Questions: **Hvordan siger man "thank you" på dansk?**¶• Subordinate clauses: **Appetitten kommer, mens man spiser.** (Appetite comes with eating.)¶• Object form **en**: **Det kan gøre en nervøs.** (It can make you nervous.) Possessive **ens**: **At rejse udvider ens horisont.** (Traveling broadens your horizons.)¶Do not confuse **man** (one) with **mand** (a man, husband). Writing mand for man is a classic mistake.¶English speakers overuse du in general statements. Danish also uses du in speech, but man is neutral and safe in writing, proverbs and advice. Inside the clause, a reflexive refers back to man: **Man skal tage sig sammen.**
C1|pronouns|Reflexive possessive: sin, sit, sine|503,466,794,654,1174,725,675,750,777,608|Use sin/sit/sine when the owner is the subject; use hans/hendes/deres for someone else.|The reflexive possessive refers back to the **subject of its own clause**. It agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner.¶T:Thing owned¦Form¦Example//en-word¦sin¦**sin far**//et-word¦sit¦**sit job**//plural¦sine¦**sine børn**¶• Subject owns it: **Han tager sig af sin syge mor.** (He takes care of his sick mother.) **Hun har opdraget sine børn til at være selvstændige.**¶• Different owner: **Vi fejrer deres diamantbryllup.** (We are celebrating their anniversary, someone else's.) Here **deres**, not sit.¶• Fixed phrases: **Livet på landet har sine fordele og ulemper.** (Country life has its pros and cons.) **Vi er gået hver til sit.** (We went our separate ways.)¶• Idioms: **Han har kastet sine øjne på hende.** (He has his eye on her.)¶Mistake: **Han tog hans bil** when hans is the subject himself. Say **Han tog sin bil.** Sin is never part of the subject: not **Sin bror kommer**.¶Tip: with jeg, du and vi use the normal possessives min, din, vores. In everyday speech many Danes use **deres** for plural owners, but sine/sit is the standard in writing.
C1|pronouns|Emphatic and reflexive selv|957,980,1424,1197,1925,2183,2349,1526,193,245|Selv adds emphasis (myself, by yourself); mig selv, dig selv, sig selv reinforce a reflexive object.|**Selv** works in two ways.¶• Emphasis, "by myself": **Jeg har selv bagt kagen.** (I baked the cake myself.) **Vi har selv stået for renoveringen.** (We did the renovation ourselves.) **Udlejeren skal selv bo der.** (The landlord will live there himself.)¶• Reinforced reflexive: **mig selv, dig selv, sig selv, os selv**. **Jeg overgik mig selv.** (I outdid myself.) **Han overgik sig selv.** **Jeg forkæler mig selv en gang imellem.** (I treat myself now and then.)¶• Fixed phrases: **Det siger sig selv.** (That goes without saying.) **Hold det for dig selv.** (Keep it to yourself.)¶Compare the plain reflexive **sig**: **Han barberer sig** (He shaves) vs. **Han ser sig selv i spejlet** (He sees himself in the mirror), which stresses himself.¶Other uses:¶• **Selv tak!** (You are welcome!)¶• **selvom** (even though): **Selvom det regner, går vi en tur.**¶• **selve** (the very): **selve ideen** (the very idea).¶Tip: with some verbs the plain reflexive is enough: **Han vasker sig** (not vasker sig selv).
C1|pronouns|Reciprocal hinanden|98,136,235,300,305,577,585,764,491,398|Hinanden means each other; it is invariable, never a subject, and takes a preposition like any object.|**Hinanden** (each other, one another) never changes and works as an object or after a preposition. The subject must be plural.¶• **Vi har ikke set hinanden i lang tid.** (We have not seen each other in a long time.)¶• **Hvis jeg husker rigtigt, mødte vi hinanden i Wien.** (If I remember right, we met in Vienna.)¶• After prepositions: **Vi er meget knyttet til hinanden.** (We are very close.) **Vi har kendt hinanden siden skoletiden.**¶• Verbs: **De to kan ikke udstå hinanden.** (Those two can not stand each other.) **Vi har ikke mere at sige hinanden.**¶• Possessive: **hinandens** (each other's): **De læser hinandens breve.**¶Not the same as the reflexive **sig**. **De så sig** can mean they saw themselves, while **De så hinanden** means they saw each other.¶Tip: English "each other" and "one another" both become hinanden. A related phrase is **hver for sig** (separately): **Hver for sig, tak.** Do not say **hinanden** as a subject: **De elsker hinanden** is fine, **Hinanden elsker** is not.
C1|pronouns|Free relatives: den der, det der, alt hvad|2791,4356,4527,5163,154,4907,5871,2699,237,4601|Den, der = whoever; det, der/som = what. Alt, hvad = everything that. The clause is subordinate, so it is set off by commas.¶• **Den, der** = the one who, whoever: **Den, der rejser, har noget at fortælle.** (Anyone who travels has stories to tell.) **Den, der tier, samtykker.** (Silence gives consent.)¶• **Det, der / det, som** = what, that which: **Det er ikke det, der er pointen.** (That is not the point.) **Musik udtrykker det, som ord ikke kan sige.** (Music expresses what words can not say.)¶• After **alt** (everything) use **hvad**: **Man skal ikke tro på alt, hvad der står på nettet.** (You should not believe everything on the internet.)¶Der can only be a subject. If the relative word is the object, use **som** or drop it: **Det, jeg vil frem til, er følgende.** (What I am getting at is the following.)¶Mistake: using **hvad** after **det** (**det hvad er vigtigt**). Say **det, der er vigtigt**.¶Tip: in speech the commas become a short pause. Proverbs love this pattern: **Den, der hviler, ruster.**
C1|pronouns|Quantifiers: enhver, hver, begge, som helst|349,736,941,1101,1142,2976,3137,2779,601,3124|Enhver/hver mean every, begge means both, and som helst means any at all. C1|adjectives|Comparison and irregular forms|178,285,975,1128,1386,1134,1149,325,1314,996|Add -ere/-est, use mere/mest for long adjectives, and learn god, dårlig, meget, lidt and mange.|• Regular: **stor, større, størst**; **lang, længere, længst**. C1|adjectives|Jo ... desto: the more, the more|5515,6114,6115,6125,1149|Jo + comparative, desto/jo + comparative links two parallel changes; the second clause has verb-second order.|Use **jo + comparative ... desto/jo + comparative** for "the more ... the more".¶• **Jo længere vi venter, desto dyrere bliver det.** (The longer we wait, the more expensive it gets.)¶• **Jo mere vi ved, desto mere indser vi, hvad vi ikke ved.** (The more we know, the more we realise what we do not know.)¶• **Jo mere man tænker over det, jo mere kompliceret bliver det.** (The more you think about it, the more complicated it gets.)¶Word order: the first part is a subordinate clause with normal subject-verb order (**jo længere vi venter**). The second part is a main clause, so the verb comes right after the comparative phrase (inversion): **desto dyrere bliver det**.¶Both **jo** and **desto** are fine in the second half. **Desto** is a little more formal and common in writing.¶Related: **mere og mere** (more and more, as in Kvarteret bliver mere og mere gentrificeret) and the fixed phrase **ikke desto mindre** (nevertheless): **Ikke desto mindre bør vi prøve.**¶Tip: do not use "the" (den, det) with the comparatives here.
C1|adjectives|Adjectives used as nouns|793,2159,3494,1265,179,3392,4517,4581,4583,5276|Det + adjective names an abstract idea; de + adjective means a group of people.|An adjective can stand alone as a noun after a determiner.¶• **Det vigtigste** (the most important thing): **Familien er det vigtigste i livet.** **Det vigtigste er at være med.** (Taking part is what counts.)¶• **Det samme** (the same): **Jeg tager det samme.** (I will have the same.)¶• **Det værste** (the worst): **Det værste er overstået.** (I am over the worst.)¶• **Det ene ... det andet**: **Det ene udelukker ikke det andet.** (One does not rule out the other.)¶• Groups of people with **de**: **de unge** (young people), **de ældre** (older people), **de svageste** (the most vulnerable), **de rigeste ti procent** (the richest ten percent).¶The adjective ends in **-e** (or **-ste** in the superlative) and refers to a group, so it is plural.¶Mistake: adding a noun like ting is not needed in general statements: **det vigtigste**, not den vigtigste ting.¶Tip: English "one" (the red one) is expressed by a bare adjective with the right article: **den røde** (en-word), **det røde** (et-word).
C1|adjectives|Participles used as adjectives|309,334,993,772,1587,2325,4579,4428,5148,644|Present participles in -ende work as adjectives and adverbs and never change; past participles agree.|The present participle (**-ende**) can be an adjective or an adverb. C1|preps|Compound prepositions: på grund af, trods, i stedet for|3584,2646,5148,6123,6126,3086,4955,992,4269,4878|Multi-word prepositions give reasons and contrasts in formal writing; they are followed by a noun phrase.|• **På grund af** (because of): **Klinikken er lukket på grund af ferie.** (The practice is closed because of vacation.) **Han blev frifundet på grund af manglende beviser.**¶• **Trods / til trods for** (despite): **Trods alle anstrengelser lykkedes det ikke.** (Despite all efforts, it did not succeed.) **Det til trods blev projektet videreført.** (Despite that, the project was continued.)¶• **I stedet for** (instead of): before a noun or **at + infinitive**: **Jeg får den repareret i stedet for at smide den ud.** (I am having it repaired instead of throwing it away.)¶• **I forhold til** (in relation to, compared with): **Vi halter bagud i forhold til tidsplanen.** (We are lagging behind schedule.)¶• **På bekostning af** (at the expense of): **Vi lever på bekostning af de kommende generationer.**¶T:Compound¦Use//på grund af¦cause//trods, til trods for¦concession//i stedet for¦alternative//i forhold til¦comparison//på bekostning af¦cost¶Mistake: following **på grund af** with a full clause. C1|preps|Adjective + preposition: stolt af, bange for, glad for|501,502,538,3701,1751,1776,2152,3463,61,498|Adjectives take fixed prepositions that rarely match English: stolt af, bekymret for, forelsket i.|Many adjectives require a particular preposition, so learn them as chunks.¶T:Chunk¦Meaning//stolt af¦proud of//bekymret for¦worried about//bange for¦afraid of//glad for¦glad about, fond of//forelsket i¦in love with//tilfreds med¦satisfied with//træt af¦tired of//afhængig af¦dependent on¶• **Jeg er stolt af dig.** (I am proud of you.) **Jeg er bekymret for min far.** (I am worried about my father.)¶• **Jeg er blevet rigtig glad for hende.** (I have grown very fond of her.) **Jeg er glad for at se dig.** (I am happy to see you.)¶• **Jeg er bange for at være alene.** takes **at + infinitive**, like English "of being".¶• **Jeg er træt af det her job.** (I am fed up with this job.) **Jeg er blevet forelsket i ham.**¶Mistake: using the English preposition: not **bange af**, not **stolt for**. C1|conj|Concession: selvom, skønt, uanset, trods|2694,6121,6122,6124,6123,6126,6393,6130,337|Selvom and skønt open a concessive clause; trods and uanset take a noun phrase.|Concessive links introduce something that contrasts with the main statement.¶• **Selvom / selv om** (even though) + subordinate clause: **Jeg har allerede udlængsel, selvom jeg lige er kommet hjem.** (I already have wanderlust, even though I just got back.) In the fronted version the verb inverts: **Selv om målet er rigtigt, er vejen forkert.**¶• **Skønt** (although, formal): **Skønt tallene ser gode ud, er jeg stadig forsigtig.**¶• **Uanset** (regardless of): **Uanset kritikken holder regeringen fast ved planen.**¶• **Trods / til trods for** + noun: **Trods alle anstrengelser lykkedes det ikke.** (Despite all efforts, it did not succeed.) **Det til trods blev projektet videreført.** **Livet er dejligt, trods alt.**¶• **Ganske vist ..., men**: **Det er ganske vist rigtigt, men det er ikke nok.** (That is true, but it is not enough.)¶• **Hvordan det end forholder sig, bør vi gå i gang.** (Be that as it may, we should get started.)¶Mistake: **selvom** + noun (selvom regnen). C1|conj|Paired conjunctions: både ... og, hverken ... eller|595,1396,3987,4679,5747,5990,6112,6113,6110,6111|Både ... og, hverken ... eller and ikke kun ... men også link two parts of equal weight.|These paired links join two equal parts.¶• **Både ... og** (both ... and): **Vi deler både glæder og sorger.** (We share both joys and sorrows.) **Teknologien er både en velsignelse og en forbandelse.** **Jeg føler mig fremmed både her og der.**¶• **Hverken ... eller** (neither ... nor): **Hverken den ene eller den anden løsning er perfekt.** **Jeg ved hverken ud eller ind.** (I am at a complete loss.) **Det gør hverken fra eller til.**¶• **Ikke kun ... men også** (not only ... but also): **Ikke kun omkostningerne, men også arbejdet er enormt.**¶• **Dels ... dels** (partly ... partly, for one thing ... for another): **Dels sparer man penge, dels skåner man miljøet.**¶• **Både** can start a sentence: **Både fra et økologisk og et økonomisk synspunkt kan det betale sig.**¶Rules: the two parts have the same form (two nouns, two phrases). C1|conj|Conditions: hvis, medmindre, forudsat at|178,6116,6117,108,368,319,3006,136,177,300|Hvis opens a condition, medmindre means unless, and forudsat at means provided that.|Danish has several ways to state conditions.¶• **Hvis** (if): **Gør det noget, hvis jeg åbner vinduet?** (Do you mind if I open the window?) **Sig til, hvis der ændrer sig noget.** (Let me know if anything changes.) **Tag det ikke ilde op, hvis jeg går tidligt.**¶• **Medmindre** (unless): **Medmindre du har en bedre idé.** **Medmindre vi finder en bedre løsning.**¶• **Forudsat at** (provided that): **Forudsat at alle er med, kan det lykkes.**¶• **Hvis ... ikke** often replaces unless: **Kan jeg levere den tilbage, hvis den ikke passer?** (Can I return it if it does not fit?)¶• Fronted conditions invert: **Hvis jeg ikke tager fejl, har vi mødt hinanden før.** **Hvis jeg husker rigtigt, mødte vi hinanden i Wien.**¶Unreal conditions use the past or pluperfect: **Hvis jeg bare havde vidst det!**¶Mistake: **hvis** is not **om**. C1|conj|Time clauses: mens, da, når, før|1375,1378,2221,3016,4103,4108,294,1036,689,701|Mens = while, da = once in the past, når = repeated or future, før = before; the verb stays last.|Choose the right link according to timing.¶• **Mens** (while, at the same time): **Mens du laver mad, dækker jeg bord.** (While you cook, I will set the table.) **Appetitten kommer, mens man spiser.**¶• **Da** (when, a single event in the past): **Jeg brækkede armen, da jeg stod på ski.** (I broke my arm skiing.) **Jeg var ikke hjemme, da budet kom.** **Da jeg var lille, havde jeg en hund.**¶• **Når** (when, repeated or future): **Hun ringer kun, når hun skal bruge noget.** (She only calls when she needs something.) **Sig til, når du har tid.**¶• **Før** (before): **Der er ingen dessert, før du har spist dine grøntsager.** (No dessert until you have eaten your vegetables.) **Vi skal sætte lejligheden i stand, før vi flytter ud.**¶• **Så snart** (as soon as): **Jeg vender tilbage, så snart jeg kan.**¶• **Siden** (since): **De har været som ler og langhalm, siden de var små.**¶Mistake: **når** for a single past event. English "when I was little" is **da**, not **når**.¶Tip: in a subordinate clause, the verb comes after the subject and the adverbs: **da jeg ikke kunne**.

C1|neg|Understatement: ikke helt, ikke ligefrem, ikke spor|257,316,1395,1448,3335,396,3673,4902,2547,3435|Ikke + helt/ligefrem/spor softens a judgment; Danes often say less than they mean.|Danes tend to understate. C1|neg|Tag questions and hedged checks|116,202,277,148,106,236|Ikke?, vel? and eller? turn a statement into a request for confirmation; vel adds a hopeful tone.|Danish has no fixed tag like English "isn't it"; it uses short particles.¶• **ikke?** (right?): **Du laver sjov, ikke?** (You are joking, right?)¶• **vel?** (surely?): **Vi kender vist ikke hinanden, vel?** (We have not met yet, have we?) **Jeg forstyrrer vel ikke?** (I am not disturbing you, am I?) C1|punct|Comma before subordinate clauses|91,94,106,108,113,124,125,136,1120,1378|Danish puts a comma before every subordinate clause (at, om, som, hvis, når, mens...).|Danish comma rules are logical: **a comma before every subordinate clause**, and one after a subordinate clause that opens the sentence. This includes **at**-clauses, unlike English "that".¶• **at / om**: **Jeg ville bare sige, at jeg er glad.** (I just wanted to say that I am happy.) **Jeg ville spørge dig, om du har tid.** **Er det rigtigt, at du flytter?**¶• **hvis, når, mens**: **Gør det noget, hvis jeg åbner vinduet?** **Sig til, når du har tid.** **Appetitten kommer, mens man spiser.**¶• Question words: **Jeg er ligeglad med, hvad vi laver.** (I do not care what we do.) **Kan du sige mig, hvor banegården er?**¶• Result clauses: **Væggene er så tynde, at man kan høre hvert ord.**¶• A fronted clause is closed by a comma: **Hvis jeg ikke tager fejl, har vi mødt hinanden før.** (If I am not mistaken, we have met before.) The verb of the main clause comes first (V2).¶Mistake: writing no comma before at (Jeg tror at det er sandt). In Danish it is mandatory: **Jeg tror, at det er sandt.**¶Tip: when in doubt, ask whether the clause has its own finite verb and a conjunction or question word. If so, put a comma before it.
C1|punct|Comma before men and between main clauses|159,190,317,320,537,653,997,1778,983,1131|A comma always goes before men; og and eller take a comma only if a new subject begins the second main clause.|• Comma before **men** (but): **Jeg vil ikke være indiskret, men hvor gammel er du?** (I do not want to be indiscreet, but how old are you?) **Det er lidt pinligt, men jeg har glemt dit navn.**¶• Also when only a word or phrase follows: **Lejligheden har charme, men ingen komfort.** **Jeg har tilgivet ham, men ikke glemt.** **Stedet er lille, men godt.**¶• Between main clauses joined by **men**: **Han går mig på nerverne, men jeg elsker ham.** **Det er ikke optimalt, men det virker.**¶• **Og, eller** (and, or): no comma if both parts share the subject; a comma is optional but common if a new subject begins: **Jeg har låst mig ude, og låsesmeden er dyr.**¶• Also a comma before **for** (because) and **thi** (formal) when they link main clauses.¶Mistake: leaving out the comma before men, as often happens in English.¶Tip: in lists, Danish does not use a comma before the last item: **Jeg køber æg, mælk og brød.** The English "Oxford comma" is wrong in Danish.
C1|punct|Compound words: one word, not two|587,1087,1549,1058,1806,3490,4681,4794,4407,4675|Danish compounds are written as one word; splitting them (særskrivning) changes the meaning and looks wrong.|Danish compounds are written as **one word**, unlike English.¶• **opbevaringsplads** (storage space), **produktionsforhold** (production conditions), **familiemenneske** (family man), **forretningsrejse** (business trip), **sundhedsforsikring** (health insurance), **arbejdspladser** (jobs).¶• Linking letters: -s- is common (**forretningsrejse, opbevaringsplads**), -e- often (**familiemenneske**). Learn them with the word.¶• The last part sets the gender and the plural: **en rengøringsplan, flere arbejdspladser**.¶Mistake: **særskrivning**, writing two words: **opbevarings plads**, **sundheds forsikring**. It looks wrong to Danish readers and can be ambiguous.¶Hyphens appear with abbreviations, numbers and foreign words: **CO2-udledningen**, **IT-sikkerheden**, **Michelin-stjerne**, **MUS-samtale**. Also for a shared second part: **vuggestue- og børnehavepladser** (nursery and kindergarten places).¶Tip: if you hear a long word, it is probably a single compound. Compounds also take the suffix at the end: **affaldssorteringen, huslejen**.
C1|style|Reporting speech and opinions|3882,1856,6058,3952,4919,5269,5289,6055,2367,4398|Reported speech uses sige, mene, foreslå + at; the clause keeps subordinate order; hearsay uses efter sigende.|In Danish indirect speech, the reporting verb is followed by **at** and a subordinate clause (or the **at** is dropped).¶• Opinions: **Jeg mener, at vi bør vente.** (I think we should wait.) **Mange mener, at indenrigsflyvninger burde forbydes.** (Many think short-haul flights should be banned.)¶• Saying: **Nogle siger, at investeringer i fremtiden retfærdiggør ny gæld.** (Some say that investments in the future justify new debt.) **Sammenfattende kan man sige, at det kan betale sig.**¶• Suggesting: **Jeg foreslår, at vi stemmer om det.** **Derfor foreslår jeg, at vi venter og ser.**¶• Feelings and evidence: **Min mavefornemmelse siger mig, at der er noget lusk.** (My gut tells me something is fishy.)¶• Direct quotes put the reporting clause after: **I morgen er der også en dag, sagde hun roligt.** **Sport er mord, sagde Churchill efter sigende.**¶Rules: the tense usually shifts back after a past reporting verb (**Hun sagde, at hun var træt**), and sentence adverbs stand before the verb (**at han ikke kommer**).¶Tip: for distance or hearsay use **efter sigende**, **ifølge** (according to) or **påstå** (claim): **Ifølge avisen ...**
C1|style|Hedging and tact: med al respekt, hvis jeg må|177,136,300,314,315,316,317,576,1590,6184|Fixed polite frames let you disagree, ask or be frank without causing offence.|Danish politeness often comes through fixed frames rather than through the verb.¶• Admitting: **Hvis jeg skal være ærlig, havde jeg mine tvivl.** (If I am honest, I had doubts.)¶• Checking: **Hvis jeg ikke tager fejl, har vi mødt hinanden før.** (If I am not mistaken, we have met before.) **Hvis jeg husker rigtigt, mødte vi hinanden i Wien.**¶• Asking leave: **Hvis du tillader, vil jeg gerne tilføje noget.** (If you will allow me, I would like to add something.)¶• Disagreeing: **Med al respekt, det ser jeg anderledes.** (With all due respect, I see it differently.) **Med al mulig respekt, det er ikke helt rigtigt.**¶• Warning of a delicate remark: **Jeg vil ikke være indiskret, men hvor gammel er du?** **Mellem os sagt, jeg tænker ikke særlig meget om hendes nye kæreste.** (Between you and me, I do not think much of her new boyfriend.)¶• Correcting: **Helt præcist er det ikke korrekt.** (Strictly speaking, that is not correct.)¶• Reassuring: **Bare gør dig ingen ulejlighed!** (Don't go to any trouble!)¶Tip: Danish tact favours understatement and humour. Combine frames with **lige** and **bare** to sound natural: **Jeg ville bare lige sige ...**
C1|style|Formal writing: letters, e-mail and announcements|1845,1713,1651,1973,6334,6336,369,6335,6348,6355|Formal Danish uses set phrases such as vedhæftet, venlig hilsen and vi beklager.|Formal writing relies on fixed formulas.¶• Opening and attachments: **Vedhæftet finder du tilbuddet.** (Please find the offer attached.) **Vedhæftet sender jeg dig referatet.** (Attached I am sending you the minutes.)¶• Apology and bad news: **Vi beklager ulejligheden.** (We apologise for the inconvenience.) **Vi må desværre meddele dig, at stillingen allerede er besat.** (We regret to inform you that the position has already been filled.)¶• Gratitude and requests: **Jeg ville være dig meget taknemmelig, hvis du kunne hjælpe mig.** (I would be very much obliged if you could help me.)¶• Service: **Din henvendelse vil blive behandlet hurtigst muligt.** (Your request will be processed as quickly as possible.) **Jeg står altid til rådighed.** (I am at your disposal at any time.)¶• Closing: **Med venlig hilsen** (Kind regards), **Jeg ser frem til at høre fra dig.** **Vi ønsker dig alt det bedste i din videre karriere.**¶T:Part¦Phrase//Opening¦Kære ... (Dear ...)//Closing¦Med venlig hilsen//Short closing¦Venlig hilsen, Mvh¶Tip: write **Med venlig hilsen** with no comma after it in letters, and keep the verb in second place in each sentence. Use full forms (**jeg har**, not j'har) and avoid slang.
C1|style|Du and De: informal and formal address|1291,1405,1432,1589,231,232,233|Du is the normal address in Danish; De/Dem/Deres is rare, old-fashioned and very formal.|Danish speakers use **du** to nearly everyone: friends, colleagues, bosses, customers, even the royal family in daily life. The formal **De** (capitalised) is rare today.¶T:Form¦Informal¦Formal//subject¦du¦De//object¦dig¦Dem//possessive¦din, dit, dine¦Deres¶• Formal address in service language: **Kunne De anbefale mig noget?** (Could you recommend something?) **Kan De lade være med løgene?** **Hvad anbefaler De til?** **Hvad må jeg byde Dem?** (What can I offer you?)¶• Switching to du: **Må jeg sige du til dig?** (May I use "du" with you?) **Skal vi ikke bare sige du?** (Shall we switch to du?) **Du må gerne sige du til mig.** (You are welcome to call me du.)¶Always capitalise **De, Dem, Deres** in formal address. Do not confuse with **de** (they), **dem** (them) and **deres** (their).¶Mistake: using **De** with strangers. Many Danes will find it stiff, so start with **du** unless you are writing a very formal letter, speaking to elderly people or in old-fashioned service language.¶Tip: use **vi** for we, **I** for you plural, and **man** for general statements.
